title: NPR interview examines Democrats' foreign policy direction after midterm win
content: NPR host Rob Schmitz interviewed Thomas Wright, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, regarding Wright’s recent Foreign Affairs article, “The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy.” The conversation focused on the piece’s analysis of how Democrats might shape U.S. foreign policy following their midterm election victory.
summary: NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Thomas Wright, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. They discuss Wright's Foreign Affairs article titled The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy.
author: NPR Politics

title: Heavy rain floods around 70,000 tents in Gaza, worsening humanitarian situation
content:
Heavy rain began hitting Gaza on Saturday, marking the start of the first winter storm affecting the territory. Within 12 hours, reports indicated that roughly 70,000 tents used by displaced families were flooded.

Humanitarian officials warned that the flooding could worsen conditions for hundreds of thousands of people living in temporary camps that lack adequate protection from rain and cold.
summary: Heavy rain began hitting Gaza on Saturday, marking the first winter storm affecting the area. About 70,000 tents were flooded within 12 hours, prompting warnings of a worsening humanitarian situation for hundreds of thousands of displaced people in temporary camps lacking adequate protection.
author: Guardian Environment

title: US records over 5,000 measles cases, highest in 35 years
content: The United States has recorded more than 5,000 measles cases this year, the highest number in 35 years, according to an official count released on Friday. The data reflects the nation’s most severe measles outbreak in three and a half decades.
summary: The United States has recorded more than 5,000 measles cases this year. This is the highest number in 35 years, according to an official count released Friday.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study identifies unknown mechanism driving therapy resistance in advanced prostate cancer
content: A multi‑institutional collaborative study led by researchers at the University of Chicago and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center has identified a previously unknown biological mechanism that controls cell identity and treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer.
summary: A multi‑institutional collaborative study led by researchers at the University of Chicago and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center identified a previously unknown biological mechanism. The mechanism controls cell identity and treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study finds higher parkinsonism rates in middle‑aged and older adults with autism
content: A new study finds that middle‑aged and older adults with autism are more likely to have co‑occurring parkinsonism than adults without autism or intellectual disability. The research was led by George Washington University investigators in the Department of Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences.
summary: Researchers at George Washington University’s Department of Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences reported that middle‑aged and older adults with autism are more likely to have co‑occurring parkinsonism than adults without autism or intellectual disability. The study compared these groups to adults lacking autism and intellectual disability.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Earth's gravity may have sustained early moon's volcanic activity
content:
New analysis of lunar material brought back by China’s Chang’e‑5 mission shows that some of the rock formed about 2 billion years ago and bears characteristics of volcanic origin. This finding challenges the conventional view that the Moon cooled quickly after the giant impact that created it around 4.5 billion years ago, leaving only occasional asteroid impacts to modify its surface.

Researchers suggest that Earth’s gravity may have helped sustain the Moon’s early volcanic activity longer than expected, allowing magma to erupt as late as 2 billion years ago. The Chang’e‑5 samples provide direct evidence that volcanic processes persisted well after the Moon’s initial formation.
summary: The moon is generally thought to have cooled quickly after forming from a giant impact with Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. However, lunar material returned by the Chang'e‑5 mission dates to roughly 2 billion years ago and shows evidence of volcanic origin, suggesting Earth’s gravity may have kept the moon’s interior active.
author: Phys.org

title: Hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer simulates Aharonov‑Bohm effect in lattice gauge theory
content: A recent Nature Physics paper reports that researchers have used a hybrid trapped‑ion quantum computer to simulate a lattice gauge theory and observe the Aharonov‑Bohm effect. The study demonstrates interference arising from magnetic flux in the simulated system.
summary: Researchers demonstrated the Aharonov‑Bohm effect in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory. The demonstration used a hybrid trapped‑ion quantum computer and was reported in a new Nature Physics study.
author: Phys.org

title: Different genres enable doctoral students to tailor writing for new audiences
content:
Different text genres place distinct demands on writers. An academic abstract, a blog post, and a public outreach article each require a unique approach.

Readers’ prior knowledge, the purpose of the text, and what needs explaining vary across these genres. Consequently, mastering one type of writing does not automatically equip a doctoral student to write another effectively.
summary: Academic abstracts, blog posts and public outreach articles each place distinct demands on writers. Because readers’ prior knowledge, text purpose and explanatory needs vary, mastering one genre does not automatically ensure ability to write another.
author: Phys.org

title: Insects provide diverse ecosystem services beyond food, from pollination to waste decomposition
content: Insects number at least 14 million species worldwide and sustain the natural world through highly diverse roles. Scientists refer to their contributions as “ecosystem services.” For instance, bees and hoverflies pollinate wildflowers and agricultural crops, while dung beetles decompose manure and other waste materials.
summary: There are at least 14 million insect species on Earth that perform many ecosystem services. Bees and hoverflies pollinate wildflowers and agricultural crops, and dung beetles decompose manure and other waste materials.
author: Phys.org

title: Student documents rare wild cat in Carson National Forest, NM
content: William Grooms used dozens of motion‑sensing cameras during the summer to document wildlife across Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. This was his first field season collecting photos for a two‑year study aimed at understanding how forest structure influences biodiversity in the Southern Rocky Mountains.
summary: William Grooms, a student, captured evidence of a rare wild cat in Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. He used dozens of motion‑sensing cameras during his first summer field season for a two‑year study of how forest structure influences biodiversity in the Southern Rocky Mountains.
author: Phys.org

title: Space weather drives auroras and poses risk to power grids
content: An aurora appears as green or red curtains rippling across the night sky, producing a spectacular light show. When viewed from the ground, the display may seem far away and disconnected from anything happening on Earth’s surface. The title notes that space weather powers these auroras and also threatens power grids on the ground.
summary: An aurora appears as green or red curtains rippling across the night sky. The same space weather that powers these light displays can also threaten power grids on the ground.
author: Phys.org

title: JWST finds 104 magnified stellar events in Dragon galaxy, doubling prior record
content:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) enabled a team of astronomers to identify 104 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy, located roughly 6.5 billion light‑years from Earth. This count more than doubles the prior record of 44 such detections in the same galaxy.

These magnified events highlight some of the most luminous stars and suggest the presence of dark matter. The study therefore provides a rare glimpse of the Dragon’s stellar population and offers a potential clue to the nature of dark matter.
summary: Using JWST, astronomers identified 104 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy about 6.5 billion light‑years away. The count more than doubles the previous record of 44 detections and offers a rare view of the galaxy’s luminous stars and a possible hint of dark matter.
author: Phys.org

title: Liquid-assisted crystal growth cuts perovskite defects for efficient solar cells and LEDs
content: A research team led by Professor Seong Sik Shin of the SKKU Advanced Institute of Nanotechnology at Sungkyunkwan University, working with the Korea Research Institute of Chemical Technology, the University of California, San Diego and Princeton University, has created a next‑generation perovskite semiconductor thin film that exhibits dramatically reduced defects. The team employed a liquid‑assisted crystal‑growth method to achieve the lower defect density. Using this same material platform, they demonstrated both high‑performance solar cells and light‑emitting diodes.
summary: Liquid-assisted crystal growth cuts perovskite defects for efficient solar cells and LEDs.
author: Phys.org

title: Broccoli compound may aid treatment of Friedreich ataxia
content: Scientists have identified a naturally occurring compound in broccoli that may combat Friedreich ataxia, a genetic disease that progressively harms the nervous system. The compound appears to boost a vital protein and protect nerve cells, raising hopes for an affordable therapy. However, clinical trials are still required to confirm its effectiveness in patients.
summary: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, but clinical trials are still needed to confirm its effectiveness in patients.
author: Science Daily

title: Low testosterone tied to 18% higher cancer death risk in study of 26,000 men
content: A large international study that followed more than 26,000 men found that men with very low testosterone levels faced an 18 % higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. The analysis showed no clear association between testosterone levels and prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones were linked to that disease. Researchers noted that testosterone levels falling below 8.6 nmol/L might serve as an early warning sign of future health risks.
summary: A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find structural brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
content: Scientists report that sleep disorders are linked to structural changes in brain regions governing attention, decision‑making and emotions, which may explain how disrupted sleep influences everyday thinking and behavior. The conclusion comes from an analysis of 57 brain‑imaging studies that identified both shared and disorder‑specific patterns, suggesting potential pathways for more targeted treatments.
summary: Scientists discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.
author: Science Daily

title: Humans emit over 2 billion tonnes of CO2 yearly from metabolism, up 74% in 30 years
content: Humans collectively exhale more than 2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide each year as they convert food into energy, a level that has risen 74 % over the past three decades, primarily due to population growth. Because this CO₂ is part of the natural carbon cycle rather than fossil‑fuel emissions, scientists say that more precise measurement of human respiration could help refine climate models.
summary: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide each year by converting food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades driven largely by population growth. Scientists note that this exhaled CO2 is part of the natural carbon cycle and that better measurement could improve climate models.
author: Science Daily

title: Psilocybin shown to rapidly create and strengthen new brain connections in mice
content: Scientists have discovered that psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, can rapidly reshape the brain by generating new neural connections and strengthening existing ones. In experiments with mice, the drug exhibited different effects in healthy animals compared to those experiencing chronic stress, suggesting it may help repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. The researchers also identified a method to induce this neural rewiring without producing the behavioral response typically linked to psychedelic effects.
summary: Researchers discovered that psilocybin rapidly reshapes the brain by forming new neural connections and strengthening them. The drug acted differently in healthy versus chronically stressed mice and could be triggered to induce rewiring without the behavioral response linked to psychedelic effects.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists generate record 300‑attosecond X‑ray flashes in tiny spot
content: Scientists have generated X‑ray flashes that last only 300 attoseconds and concentrate unprecedented power into an extremely small focal spot. The achievement is described as a breakthrough that may enable direct observation of electrons in motion and could allow control of the ultrafast processes underlying chemical reactions.
summary: Scientists have created record‑breaking X‑ray flashes lasting 300 attoseconds that concentrate enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot. The breakthrough could provide a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find Europe was covered by open woodlands, meadows for 20 million years
content: Scientists have found that for more than 20 million years Europe was primarily covered by open woodlands, colorful meadows and large grazing animals, rather than the dense forests traditionally viewed as its natural state. The finding questions current reforestation plans, indicating that planting thick forests might damage the biodiversity that conservationists aim to preserve.
summary: Scientists uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.
author: Science Daily

title: MIT scientists create nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells to kill cancer in mice
content: MIT researchers have created nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells directly within the body, prompting them to attack cancer and harmful immune cells. In mouse studies, the approach eliminated tumors and reversed liver damage. The scientists say the method could simplify and lower the cost of immune therapies and expand treatment options for cancer and autoimmune diseases.
summary: MIT scientists have developed nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells directly inside the body to attack cancer and harmful immune cells, eliminating tumors and reversing liver damage in mouse experiments. The breakthrough could make powerful immune therapies dramatically simpler and less expensive while opening new possibilities for treating cancer and autoimmune diseases.
author: Science Daily

title: Rep‑elect Will Lawrence vows to push federal data center moratorium
content: Will Lawrence, who defeated better‑funded opponents to win Michigan’s 7th District congressional race, is now the district’s representative‑elect. He has announced plans to pursue a federal moratorium on data center construction.
summary: Will Lawrence is the representative‑elect for Michigan’s 7th District after beating better‑funded opponents. He says he will work to enact a federal moratorium on data center construction.
author: Wired

title: AI‑enhanced caregiver apps become more capable, but caregiver well‑being remains unsolved
content: Apps and platforms that assist family caregivers in managing loved‑ones’ needs are gaining new capabilities, including artificial‑intelligence features. However, the broader challenge of supporting caregivers’ own well‑being remains unresolved.
summary: The apps and platforms that help family caregivers manage their loved ones’ needs are becoming more capable. However, the broader issue of caregivers’ well‑being remains unsolved.
author: Wired

title: Fridge-hacking spree highlights IoT security risks to critical infrastructure
content: Recent hacks of blood‑lab systems and grocery‑store networks illustrate how basic security gaps in internet‑connected devices can threaten critical infrastructure. The growing “fridge‑hacking” spree is being described as a wake‑up call to address these IoT vulnerabilities.
summary: Recent hacks affecting blood labs and grocery stores are escalating. They show real risks to critical infrastructure from basic security lapses in internet-connected devices.
author: Wired

title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's ties to Chinese spy
content:
Nvidia disclosed that its board of directors is launching an independent investigation concerning CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. The probe follows reports that Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company and that Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

The investigation will be overseen by a committee of independent directors assisted by outside independent counsel. In its statement, the board emphasized that U.S. national and economic security is a paramount priority for Nvidia.
summary: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's ties to Chinese spy.
author: The Verge

title: Epic Games Launcher gains SteamOS support, says communications director
content:
In October, Epic Games announced it was investigating how to make Fortnite compatible with Valve’s Linux‑based SteamOS. At that time the Epic Games Launcher was still in preview, and SteamOS was not listed among the supported distributions.

Communications Director Jake Jones has since confirmed that SteamOS will be supported, along with several other Linux distros, in a recent interview with GamingOnLinux.

Jones explained that the new Epic Games Launcher remains in preview and that the company intends to support as many Linux distributions as possible. He noted plans to include Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more, and that the launcher will replace the AppImage with Debian/Ubuntu downloads.
summary: Epic Games Launcher, still in preview, is now confirmed to be compatible with Valve’s Linux‑based SteamOS. Communications Director Jake Jones said the launcher will also support other Linux distributions such as Fedora, Cachy, Omarchy, and more.
author: The Verge

title: Apps designed to curb doomscrolling and boost productive content
content: Breaking the habit of doomscrolling can be challenging, but a variety of apps are available that aim to redirect users toward more engaging and productive content. These tools are presented as alternatives to endless negative scrolling, offering ways to spend time on material that supports a healthier online experience.
summary: Breaking the cycle of doomscrolling is hard. Plenty of apps can help users spend more time on engaging and productive content.
author: TechCrunch

title: Pokémon card craze fuels scalper race as fans queue at London’s Forbidden Planet
content:
Fans seeking the newest Pokémon card releases are finding themselves priced out as a “cut‑throat” market, driven by hype that a young fan likened to “crypto”. The demand has turned card collecting into a race against scalpers, according to observations from the scene.

On a Friday before the 10 a.m. opening of the pop‑culture shop Forbidden Planet in central London, a line that began at 3 a.m. stretched past five other queues. Kai, who had been waiting since the early hours, said the crowd was roughly “50/50” fans and resellers despite the store’s strict sales policy.
summary: Fans trying to buy the latest Pokémon cards are being priced out in a cut‑throat market driven by hype likened to crypto. At the Friday 10 am opening of Forbidden Planet in central London, a line that started at 3 am was about half fans and half resellers, according to Kai.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Trump offers UFC boss Dana White White House press secretary position
content: Trump and White have forged a close relationship over the years, with Trump a regular attendee at UFC events and White having spoken at a number of the president's rallies.
summary: Trump offered UFC boss Dana White a role as White House press secretary. The two have a close relationship, with Trump regularly attending UFC events and White speaking at many of the president's rallies.
author: Euronews

title: Eisenkot given 28 days to form new Israeli government after elections
content: Netanyahu rival Eisenkot has been designated to try to form a new Israeli government after the recent elections. Under Israeli law, the appointed candidate has 28 days to assemble a coalition, and the president may extend this period by up to 14 days before assigning the mandate to another individual.
summary: Eisenkot, a rival of Netanyahu, has been tasked with forming a new government in Israel. He has 28 days to do so, and the president may extend the period by up to 14 days before assigning the mandate to another candidate.
author: Euronews

title: US forces strike bulk carrier in Gulf of Oman after crew ignored warnings
content: US forces reportedly struck a commercial bulk carrier in the Gulf of Oman after the crew ignored repeated warnings, according to the headline. The UKMTO maritime agency said late on Saturday that it had received a report of an incident involving a bulk carrier and military forces in the gulf.
summary: US forces struck a commercial bulk carrier in the Gulf of Oman after the crew ignored repeated warnings. The UKMTO said it had received a report of the incident involving the bulk carrier and military forces in the gulf.
author: Euronews

title: Pope Leo XIV ends Uruguay visit with women tribute, mass draws 50,000 in Florida
content:
Pope Leo XIV concluded his visit to Uruguay with a tribute to women before departing for Argentina.  

Tens of thousands gathered in Florida’s main square for the Mass under bright blue skies, some walking several kilometres to reach the site. The city’s population is about 40,000, yet the Vatican estimated 50,000 attendees.
summary: Pope Leo XIV concluded his Uruguay trip with a tribute to women before departing for Argentina. Tens of thousands, estimated at 50,000 by the Vatican, attended a Mass in Florida’s main square despite the city’s 40,000 population.
author: Euronews

title: Kraków's main square reopens a day after shooting that killed six
content: Kraków’s historic main square reopened to the public on Sunday, 8 November, just over 24 hours after a deadly shooting that left six people dead and 15 injured. Residents are lighting candles in memory of the victims, while bullet marks remain visible on café windows.
summary: Kraków's historic main square reopened to the public on Sunday, 8 November, just over 24 hours after a shooting left six people dead and 15 injured. Residents are lighting candles in memory of the victims, and bullet marks remain visible on café windows.
author: Euronews

title: Tens of thousands march in red through Amsterdam demanding stronger Dutch action on Gaza
content: A sea of red filled Amsterdam’s streets on Sunday, 8 November, as tens of thousands of demonstrators—many wearing red—marched through the city. The protest called on the Dutch government to adopt stronger measures against Israel concerning the war in Gaza.
summary: Tens of thousands of people, many dressed in red, marched through Amsterdam on Sunday 8 November. They urged the Dutch government to take stronger action against Israel over the war in Gaza.
author: Euronews

title: French tear gas use sparks calls to ban after menstrual disorder reports
content: French police have deployed tear gas extensively during recent protests across France, resulting in grievous injuries. Thousands of women have reported acutely painful periods and increased bleeding, challenging the assumption that the chemical irritant causes only minor effects.
summary: French police have extensively used tear gas during recent protests, causing grievous injuries. Thousands of women report acutely painful periods and increased bleeding, challenging the belief that tear gas has only minor effects.

title: Pope Leo XIV Urges Men to Respect Wives Amid Latin American Femicide Crisis
content: Pope Leo XIV concluded the first leg of his 12‑day Latin American tour by urging men to respect their wives. He highlighted that the region has recorded nearly 20,000 female homicide victims in the past five years, most of whom were killed by a current or former partner.
summary: Pope Leo XIV urged men to respect their wives as he wrapped up the first leg of his 12‑day tour of Latin America. The region recorded nearly 20,000 instances of women being killed over the past five years alone, most of them murdered by a current or former partner.
author: France 24

title: France says Europe will join US‑mediated Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi
content: France’s foreign minister, Jean‑Noël Barrot, announced on Sunday that France will join the upcoming Abu Dhabi peace summit aimed at ending the Ukraine war, and that European nations will be represented at the event. The talks are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday and will be mediated by the United States.
summary: France will participate in the upcoming Abu Dhabi peace talks on ending the Ukraine war, Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Sunday. Europeans will be represented at the summit, which will be held under US mediation on Tuesday and Wednesday.
author: France 24

title: Poland launches terrorism probe after shooting kills six, injures 16
content:
Poland has launched a terrorism investigation after a deadly shooting that killed six people and injured 16.

A 24‑year‑old Polish suspect, reportedly fascinated by far‑right ideologies, is under investigation for a possible extremist motive. Krakow's main square remains sealed, and two days of national mourning have been declared for the victims.
summary: Poland opened a terrorism investigation after a shooting left six dead and 16 injured. A 24‑year‑old Polish suspect, reportedly fascinated by far‑right ideologies, is being investigated, Krakow’s main square remains sealed, and two days of national mourning were declared.

title: Migrant boat sinks off Senegal, at least 34 dead
content: A migrant vessel traveling the hazardous Atlantic Ocean route from West Africa to Europe sank off Senegal’s coast, authorities said Sunday. The incident killed at least 34 people. Only one survivor has been located, and an indeterminate number of passengers remain missing.
summary: A boat carrying migrants on the hazardous Atlantic Ocean route from West Africa to Europe sank off the coast of Senegal, killing at least 34 people, authorities said Sunday. Only one survivor has been found and an indeterminate number of people remain missing.
author: France 24

title: Eisenkot tasked by Herzog to form coalition government
content: Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot was appointed by President Isaac Herzog to attempt to form a government. Lacking a clear parliamentary majority, Eisenkot faces an uphill task building a coalition with Israel’s fragmented minor parties.
summary: Israel's ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot was tapped by President Isaac Herzog to form a government. His lack of a clear majority in parliament makes coalition-building with divided minor parties an uphill struggle.

content:
Pope Leo is set to continue his South American tour by heading to Argentina for the second leg, where he is expected to attract the largest crowd of his papacy to date. The pontiff has already concluded his initial visit to Uruguay.

Colleen Dulle, Vatican Correspondent for America Magazine and co‑host of the “Inside the Vatican” podcast, will join the discussion to analyze the significance of his Latin American tour.
summary: Pope Leo is traveling to Argentina for the second leg of his South America tour after completing a visit to Uruguay. The Argentina leg is expected to draw the largest turnout of his papacy, and Vatican correspondent Colleen Dulle will analyze the tour’s significance.

title: Gadi Eisenkot begins coalition talks, reaches out to Netanyahu allies after mandate
content: Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’ Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis. Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.
summary: Gadi Eisenkot, former military chief and leader of the Yashar party, received a 28‑day mandate from President Isaac Herzog on Sunday to form a government. He said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had brought Israel to a historic crisis and is reaching out to Netanyahu’s allies to try to bridge the country’s deep polarization.

title: Polish prosecutors launch terrorism probe into Kraków market shooting
content:
Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation following a shooting in Kraków’s market square that killed six people, including a Briton, and injured 17. The 24‑year‑old gunman opened fire on Saturday afternoon, and authorities say the attack was probably inspired by far‑right ideologies.

Police confirmed on Sunday that three people were found dead at the gunman’s home: his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his sister, 21. The deaths were discovered after the Saturday attack.
summary: Prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation after a 24‑year‑old man opened fire in a busy market square in Kraków, killing six people including a Briton and wounding 17. Police said the gunman's father, mother and sister were found dead at his home.
author: Guardian World

title: UK spent £100m on unused Brexit border inspection posts, five of seven never operational
content:
The National Audit Office has revealed that the United Kingdom wasted at least £100 million of taxpayers’ money on border inspection posts that never entered service. Five of the seven facilities built in England and Wales never reached an operational stage, a result of the Conservative Party’s indecision over how to check goods after Brexit.

The audit’s broader estimate places the total cost of Brexit at about £4.7 billion. That figure includes the years‑long transformation of software used for customs declarations and other systems developed to support the UK’s exit from the single market.
summary: The UK wasted at least £100m of taxpayers’ money on “zombie” Brexit border inspection posts that were never used. Five of the seven facilities in England and Wales never reached an operational stage as Tories vacillated over plans to check goods.
author: Guardian World

title: Two Kraków police officers hailed as heroes after confronting gunman
content:
Two Polish police officers have been hailed as heroes after they pursued and detained a gunman in Kraków on Saturday, actions that prevented further casualties.  

One officer, Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, was left critically injured after a close‑range exchange of fire with the suspect. The other officer, Artur Morański, was also wounded. The suspect, a 24‑year‑old Polish national, killed six people and injured 17 in an attack believed to have been inspired by far‑right ideologies.
summary: Two Polish police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, were injured while pursuing and detaining a gunman in Kraków on Saturday. Their actions are credited with preventing further casualties after the 24‑year‑old suspect killed six and injured 17 in an attack believed to be inspired by far‑right ideologies.

title: Cold blast drops snow on Thredbo, Perisher, Mount Hotham and Mount Wellington
content:
Snow fell across parts of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania over the weekend as an unseasonal cold blast moved through Australia’s south‑east. The alpine resorts of Thredbo, Perisher and Mount Hotham each recorded snowfall on Saturday and Sunday, and snow was also reported on Kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Hobart.

Meteorologists noted that the cold snap caused temperatures to plunge, but they warned that the weather will soon shift, with warm temperatures and thunderstorms expected to follow the brief winter‑like conditions.
summary: Snow fell on Thredbo, Perisher and Mount Hotham in New South Wales and Victoria over the weekend. Snow also fell on Kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Tasmania, and forecasters say warm temperatures and thunderstorms are on the way.

title: NASA opens applications for 25th astronaut class, deadline Dec 3 2026
content: For the first time in two years, NASA is opening applications for its next astronaut class. Announcing the call at the Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC), NASA said this will be one of its most important classes yet, with the new astronauts training for low Earth orbit (LEO), lunar surface operations and future Artemis missions. According to NASA’s website, only 370 people have been selected as NASA astronaut candidates (ASCANs) since the original Mercury 7 were announced in 1959. This will be the 25th astronaut class selected in that time. Applications are open until 3 December 2026, with the selection expected in late 2027. The most recent class, NASA’s 24th, was announced in 2025 and consisted of ten new ASCANs. It also marked the first time that women outnumbered men in a NASA astronaut class. Each new astronaut group is given a nickname by the previous class. Astronaut Class 23 named the 2025 group the “Platypi”. It is not yet known what nickname the incoming class will receive. Members of the 24th astronaut class talk with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman during a training session. (Credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky) One of the Platypi is Dr Anna Menon, who became the first NASA astronaut candidate to have already flown to space on a commercial mission, Polaris Dawn. “I pinched myself when I found out that I got to join this class and get to return to the team here at NASA,” Menon said in a January 2026 interview with NSF following her selection. According to NASA, applicants must be US citizens and hold a master’s degree in a STEM field. They also need at least three years of related professional experience gained after completing that degree. Pilots can instead qualify with at least 1,000 hours of pilot-in-command time, with at least 850 of those hours in high-performance jet aircraft. All applicants must also be able to pass the NASA long-duration spaceflight astronaut physical. The master’s degree requirement can be met instead by two years of work towards a STEM doctorate, a completed medical degree, or completion of an accredited test pilot school programme. Applications must be submitted through the listing on USAJobs. Gov. The ten new ASCANs at their public announcement. (Credit: NASA/Helen Arase Vargas) The call for applications follows comments from Isaacman on NSF’s The Flame Trench that he is considering extending the life of the ISS beyond 2030 if a commercial replacement is not ready. NASA will continue to send astronauts to the ISS and to future commercial stations, all of which will need crews. NASA is also planning a base on the lunar surface, and says the new astronauts will be prepared to fly on lunar missions. Asked what advice she would give others, especially those thinking of applying to become astronauts, Menon said it is all about following your passion. “And I think that would be my piece of advice…pay attention to what you love and what you are good at and pursue that with a vengeance because what I have found is that when you do that, things tend to fall into place,” Menon said. “You tend to be most productive and fulfilled and able to contribute to the world around you in wherever life leads you.” Lead image: The ten astronauts selected as part of NASA’s 24th astronaut class. (Credit: NASA/Josh Valcarcel) The post NASA announces search for new astronauts appeared first on NASASpaceFlight. Com.
summary: NASA opens applications for 25th astronaut class, deadline Dec 3 2026.

title: NASA invites public to submit names for Dragonfly mission to Titan
content:
NASA has opened a public campaign allowing individuals to have their names included on the upcoming Dragonfly mission, which is set to explore Saturn's moon Titan. The agency launched a special events page in late October for this purpose, with a submission deadline of January 15, 2027. Selected names will be etched onto a chip that is installed on the spacecraft during its assembly. Dragonfly is described as an SUV-sized, nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA plans to launch in 2028.

Upon its expected arrival at Titan in 2034, the rotorcraft will operate for approximately 3.3 Earth years. NASA officials note that the mission does not follow an "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly is designed to fly between areas miles or kilometers apart. The spacecraft is expected to conduct one flight every one to two Titan days, a period known as a Tsol, which lasts about 16 Earth days. During its operational period, Dragonfly will visit various geologic sites, including dunes and a young impact crater named Selk.

The mission’s primary objective is to investigate Titan’s surface, which NASA describes as having an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes, and a landscape rich in organic material. Dragonfly will collect samples of surface material for analysis using a suite of scientific instruments onboard. The scientific goals of the mission include understanding prebiotic chemistry, determining if Titan possessed habitable conditions in the past, and searching for chemical indicators of life based on water or hydrocarbons.

Dragonfly will join a small group of flying craft on other worlds, following NASA’s Ingenuity mini-helicopter. Ingenuity arrived on Mars in 2021 alongside the Perseverance rover and was originally designed for five flights but completed 72 before its blades were damaged during a landing on January 18, 2024. NASA is also planning a SkyFall mission for Mars that would utilize three helicopters, with a potential launch as soon as late 2028.

While Dragonfly is not the first mission to reach Titan, it will be the first to operate on the surface for an extended period. The Huygens probe previously operated for a few hours on January 14, 2005, after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens became the first lander on an outer solar system world, measuring Titan’s atmosphere and collecting surface data. The Cassini spacecraft itself flew by Titan more than 100 times before its mission concluded in September 2017, providing long-term data from orbit.
summary: NASA opened a special events page in late October allowing the public to submit their names to be placed on a chip on the Dragonfly spacecraft, with submissions due by Jan. 15, 2027. Dragonfly, a nuclear‑powered rotorcraft, is slated for launch in 2028 to fly on Titan after arriving in 2034.

title: Planetary scientist creates lifeless Earth simulation to aid exoplanet biosignature studies
content:
A team of planetary scientists has released a computer model that simulates a rocky planet’s evolution without the influence of life. The new tool, developed by Samantha Gilbert‑Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, builds on a core‑mantle‑crust model created by Rory Barnes of the University of Washington. Gilbert‑Janizek extended the earlier work by adding the planet’s surface and atmosphere, allowing the simulation to track 19 non‑biotic properties such as stellar heat input, core‑to‑surface heat and chemical exchange, and the outflow of gases from the subsurface.

The model was run from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future, producing a lifeless world that still possessed oceans and an atmosphere. Gilbert‑Janizek used the simulation as a baseline for comparison with exoplanets, arguing that it can reveal when a planet’s atmospheric composition could be explained without life. “When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface,” she said.

Researchers can apply the bulk properties of any target planet to the model and let it run. If the simulated, lifeless atmosphere matches spectroscopic data from the James Webb Space Telescope or future 30‑meter‑plus ground‑based telescopes and NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, the planet is likely uninhabited. Conversely, a mismatch suggests that life may be altering the atmosphere, flagging the world for further study.

Barnes praised the model as “an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” noting that its simultaneous reproduction of Earth’s core, mantle, surface, and atmosphere gives confidence in future exoplanet simulations. While deviations from the model do not guarantee life, they help prioritize targets for next‑generation telescopes.

The model and its findings appear in a paper published in The Planetary Science Journal.
summary: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases.

title: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus, on Nov. 8 2005
content:
On November 8, 2005, Europe launched the Venus Express spacecraft, marking its first mission to Venus. The probe was carried into space by a Russian Soyuz rocket. This launch established the European Space Agency (ESA) as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study the planet, following the United States and the Soviet Union. Japan’s JAXA later became the fourth organization to achieve this milestone five years later.

During its operational period, the spacecraft endured harsh radiation and high atmospheric pressure for more than nine years. Venus Express observed a vortex swirling around Venus’s south pole and detected possible signs of active volcanoes. The mission also discovered that Venus generates its own auroras, which occur when solar particles interact with charged particles in the atmosphere. Near the end of the mission, controllers instructed the spacecraft to descend into Venus’s clouds, a maneuver for which it was not designed. Although the spacecraft performed well initially, it eventually stopped responding to commands and burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

The mission provided significant scientific insights into planetary evolution. According to The Planetary Society, studying Venus helps scientists understand how Earth-like planets change over time and model Earth’s climate. The Society noted that orbital studies suggest Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming an inhospitable hothouse planet. This research serves as a cautionary tale regarding the potential for dramatic climate shifts on planets throughout the galaxy.

Following the conclusion of the Venus Express mission, ESA returned to Venus in 2018. The agency used the planet’s gravity to redirect the path of BepiColombo, a joint mission with JAXA, toward the planet Mercury.
summary: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched the Venus Express spacecraft on a Russian Soyuz rocket, marking its first mission to Venus. The probe operated for more than nine years, observing a south‑pole vortex, possible volcanoes and auroras before burning up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

title: Starlog Returns as Annual Magazine for 50th Anniversary
content: "Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected. The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now. It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features. The triumphant relaunch of "Starlog" magazine happens on Nov. 13, 2026 (Image credit: Fangoria Holdings) "Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-" Star Wars " days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Terry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U. S. S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole. The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover. Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief. Three vintage "Starlog" magazine issues from my personal collection! (Image credit: Jeff Spry) "During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley. "Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build." "Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website.
summary: Starlog, a legendary sci‑fi magazine, is being resurrected as a yearly print edition on Nov. 13 2026 for its 50th anniversary, with Issue #375 available for pre‑order. The relaunch is led by Fangoria Holdings and editor‑in‑chief Annalee Newitz, following a 17‑year hiatus since the magazine went dark in 2009.

content:

content: A lot can change in five‑and‑a‑half months, but as an early winter chill descended on Wearside last week – both meteorologically and metaphorically – Sunderland were determined that some things should remain the same. content:

title: Australia to Host COP31 Negotiations in Antalya Amid Turkey Row
content:
The COP 31 climate summit has begun amid lingering tensions over its hosting arrangement. In 2021, Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, pledged to host the conference while he was still in opposition. However, complex rules delayed Australia’s bid, leading to a heated dispute with Turkey over the right to host. A final compromise placed Australia in charge of the negotiations, which will be conducted in Antalya, a city in Turkey.

The unresolved bitterness from the hosting row has left Australia’s role perceived as somewhat half‑hearted. Domestic media coverage of COP 31 has been noticeably quieter than in previous host countries. Although Albanese is scheduled to speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is expected to remain in the country only briefly.
summary: Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pledged to host COP31 in 2021, but a dispute with Turkey delayed the bid and led to a compromise that placed Australia in charge of negotiations in Antalya. Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, but is unlikely to stay long.

title: Study links Dinch plasticizer in food packaging to lower birth weight
content:
A peer‑reviewed study reports that exposure to a new generation of plasticizers, including the chemical Dinch, is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications. The research suggests these outcomes could lead to serious health problems later in life.

Din​ch, marketed as a “high safety” and nontoxic alternative to older phthalate plasticizers, is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union. The chemical also appears in children’s toys, medical devices, certain textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.
summary: A peer‑reviewed study found that exposure to the plasticizer Dinch, marketed as a “high safety” alternative and used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, is linked to lower birth weight. content:

Additionally, the pipelines are being constructed to satisfy natural gas export demand fueled by conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

title: Beef industry drops teen climate lesson on cattle methane after rancher protest
content: A beef‑industry‑funded program that aimed to teach teenagers about the role of cattle’s methane emissions in the climate crisis has been quietly removed. The lesson, which originally explained how cows contribute to global heating, was scrapped after some ranchers protested and disputed the premise that cattle affect climate change. The episode reflects a continuing, decades‑long effort by the livestock sector to influence what U.S. children are taught about cows and their environmental impact.
summary: A beef industry‑funded effort to teach teenagers about cattle’s methane emissions and climate impact was quietly scrapped. The change came after some ranchers protested, disputing the premise that cows contribute to global heating.

title: ZEUS trial shows IL-6 blocker ziltivekimab lowers inflammation but not heart events
content:
Heart researchers unpack neutral findings from ZEUS, an anti‑inflammatory clinical trial. ZEUS is a global phase 3 study led by Mass General Brigham researcher Paul Ridker, M.D. The trial tested ziltivekimab, a drug that targets interleukin‑6 (IL‑6), a downstream inflammatory molecule commonly targeted by IL‑6 inhibitors used in autoimmune disorders.

The study found that while ziltivekimab effectively lowered IL‑6 levels, it did not reduce cardiovascular event rates compared with placebo. These neutral results suggest that targeting inflammation may be less straightforward than previously thought, even though inflammation is known to causally contribute to cardiovascular disease risk.
summary: Like cholesterol, inflammation causally contributes to the risk of cardiovascular disease, but findings from the clinical trial ZEUS indicate that the road to targeting inflammation may be less straightforward than once thought. content: A study led by Queen Mary University of London reports that a new treatment may provide a lasting cure for some individuals with a common hormonal cause of high blood pressure, with effects persisting after medication is discontinued.

title: Mouse study: normal sleep may mask memory problems via ripple‑gate interneurons
content: A mouse study investigating how sleep stabilizes new memories identified specific interneurons that regulate the generation of ripples—brief bursts of electrical activity known to be essential for memory consolidation. The research, conducted by Min Xu and Wanling Peng and their team at the Institute of Neuroscience, Chinese Academy of Sciences, suggests these cells could serve as a genetic target for accessing neural circuits involved in cognitive disorders. The findings imply that sleep that appears normal may still conceal underlying memory problems.
summary: A mouse study testing how sleep stabilizes new memories identified interneurons that gate ripple bursts as a potential genetic target for circuits implicated in cognitive disorders. The research was led by Min Xu and Wanling Peng of the Institute of Neuroscience at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

content: Researchers have identified a potential driver of severe early‑onset preeclampsia, a condition that has puzzled physicians for more than two millennia. The disorder can appear as early as 20 weeks of gestation, causing sharply elevated blood pressure and endangering both mother and infant.

title: Financial incentives double quit rates for underserved smokers in national trial
content: A large national clinical trial that included Henry Ford Health found that providing financial incentives to medically underserved adults undergoing lung‑cancer screening almost doubled their smoking‑cessation rates. title: Single iron infusion boosts exercise capacity in HFpEF patients, study shows
content:
Investigators from the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute reported that a single iron infusion increased exercise capacity in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) who also have iron deficiency. The study’s results indicate that restoring iron stores may alleviate some of the physical limitations linked to this form of heart failure.

The findings were presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and were published concurrently in the journal Circulation.
summary: Investigators from the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute reported that a single iron infusion improved exercise capacity in people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and iron deficiency. title: Retatrutide cuts weight and eases knee osteoarthritis in Phase III trials
content: Two Northwestern University–led Phase III trials evaluated retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight‑loss drug, in participants with painful knee osteoarthritis who were overweight or had obesity. Across the combined trials, which enrolled more than 1,000 people, those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost roughly one‑quarter of their body weight on average. The studies focused on the drug’s impact on weight reduction among individuals for whom everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs and standing from a chair are challenging.
summary: In two Northwestern University–led Phase III trials with more than 1,000 participants, the highest dose of retatrutide caused an average weight loss of about one‑quarter of body weight. The drug also eased pain and improved function for people with overweight or obese knee osteoarthritis.

content: Researchers at City of Hope and collaborators have introduced a first‑of‑its‑kind microbiome therapy that delivers 16 selected beneficial bacteria to patients receiving donor stem cell transplants for blood cancers. summary: Researchers at City of Hope and collaborators have pioneered a new approach to preventing dangerous bloodstream infections in patients receiving donor stem cell transplants for blood cancers. title: Democrats win big House gains but have little ability to curb rising living costs
content:
Voters’ anxiety about rising prices has driven a political shift that analysts say could produce the largest swing toward Democrats since the Watergate era, giving the party its biggest House majority in almost forty years and its strongest Senate advantage since 2008. The surge is attributed to widespread concern over the cost of living, including gas, groceries, mortgages and healthcare.

title: Study examines loss vs. gain phrasing in personalized retirement savings reminders
content: Private retirement savings are gaining attention in public debate. A common approach to encouraging contributions involves framing reminders either as a warning about what could be lost by not saving or as a highlight of the benefits of saving. Studies that compare these loss‑focused and gain‑focused messages have so far yielded mixed findings, leaving it unclear which phrasing more effectively increases individuals’ saving efforts. The ongoing uncertainty underscores the need for further research on personalized savings reminders.
summary: Private retirement savings are an increasingly important topic in public debate. Research on whether loss‑framed or gain‑framed reminder messages is more effective has produced conflicting results.
author: Phys.org

title: Tropical regions lose more bird species than other areas as cities expand
content: Tropical ecosystems are noted for their exceptionally high and exuberant diversity.  Across many branches of the tree of life, biodiversity rises sharply from the poles toward the tropics—a pattern described as the latitudinal diversity gradient.  Fossil evidence indicates that this gradient has been a persistent feature for millennia.
summary: Tropical ecosystems host the greatest biodiversity on Earth. The latitudinal diversity gradient is evident across many groups and fossil evidence shows it has existed for millennia.
author: Phys.org

title: Florida chimp sanctuary uses drone to feed ape as floods swell property
content: A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary, home to about 200 apes, used a drone this week to deliver food to one animal after heavy rain flooded the property. The organization reported that the apes remained safe and that the floodwater was receding significantly by Saturday.
summary: A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary delivered food by drone to one of its 200 apes after heavy rain swamped the property. The organization said the animals remained safe and the water was receding significantly on Saturday.
author: Phys.org

title: NASA seeks applicants for new astronaut class to expand Artemis moon program
content: NASA announced that it is now accepting applications for a new astronaut class. The selected astronauts will work on expanding the Artemis program, which aims to send crews to the Moon and develop a permanent lunar base.
summary: NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class. The astronauts will help grow the Artemis program and build a permanent lunar base.
author: Phys.org

title: Stupendously large primordial black holes ruled out as dark matter source
content: A new assessment has concluded that “stupendously large” primordial black holes cannot serve as a source of the universe’s dark matter, according to the headline. Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects thought to have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe, distinguishing them from the black holes that arise when massive stars collapse. Some theories had proposed that such exceptionally massive primordial black holes might account for a significant share of dark matter, but the latest ruling rejects that possibility.
summary: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe. Some theories suggested that “stupendously large” primordial black holes could account for a significant share of dark matter, but they have now been ruled out as a dark matter source.
author: Phys.org

title: Game theory guides SETI to prioritize timing over star selection
content: Scientists working with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence are applying game‑theoretic approaches to guide their observations, emphasizing the timing of searches over the specific locations. While earlier efforts such as Project Phoenix (2012‑2015) examined roughly 1,000 sun‑like stars for technosignatures, researchers now argue that when we listen may be more crucial than where we point our instruments.
summary: Scientists are applying game theory to improve SETI's search for technosignatures. They note that timing may be more crucial than which stars are observed, as Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 sun‑like stars between 2012 and 2015.
author: Phys.org

title: Largest known ground‑dwelling bird species identified from Liang Bua cave fossils
content: Researchers have identified a new, largest‑of‑its‑kind ground‑dwelling bird species from a leg bone discovered in 2009 within the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island, the same site where Homo floresiensis was found. The fossil, dated to roughly 190,000–120,000 years ago, was initially recognized as a bird bone, set aside and later reexamined.
summary: In 2009 researchers uncovered a 190,000–120,000‑year‑old leg bone in the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island. The bone was later identified as belonging to a new, largest‑of‑its‑kind ground‑dwelling bird species from the same cave as Homo floresiensis.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists map coral colony over 1.5 km on Cocos (Keeling) Islands, among world’s largest
content:
Scientists have mapped a coral colony that stretches roughly 100 buses in length. The colony extends more than 1.5 kilometres (0.93 miles) along the outer reef of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

Researchers say the size of this formation places it among the world’s largest known coral colonies ever recorded.
summary: Scientists map coral colony over 1.5 km on Cocos (Keeling) Islands, among world’s largest.
author: Phys.org

title: COP31 may show how climate summits can still deliver modest progress
content: No one expects COP31 to prevent climate disaster, yet the summit may demonstrate that international meetings can still achieve modest, meaningful progress.
summary: No one expects COP31 to solve the climate crisis. It could provide a small taste of how international meetings can still achieve meaningful progress.
author: New Scientist

title: 24‑hour fast boosts gut bacterium that aids intestinal regeneration after radiation
content: Scientists have found that a 24‑hour fast raises levels of a beneficial gut bacterium that promotes intestinal regeneration after radiation damage. The preclinical results suggest the possibility of developing treatments to protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without the need for patients to undergo fasting.
summary: Scientists found that a 24‑hour fast raises a beneficial gut bacterium that helps intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could lead to treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.
author: Science Daily

title: Daily 2–3 Cups of Coffee Linked to Lower Dementia Risk and Better Cognition
content: A study tracking participants for as long as 43 years found that consuming two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day was associated with a dramatically lower risk of dementia and with better cognitive functioning. The protective link persisted regardless of participants’ genetic risk, while no comparable association was observed for decaffeinated coffee.
summary: A study of up to 43 years found that drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was associated with a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning. The benefits were seen regardless of genetic risk, while decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.
author: Science Daily

title: High-dose flu shot linked to 55% lower Alzheimer's risk in seniors
content:
A new study from UTHealth Houston has found that a high‑dose influenza vaccine may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease in older adults. Researchers examined data from nearly 200,000 adults aged 65 and older.  

The analysis showed that those who received the high‑dose flu shot had a nearly 55 % lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s. This reduction is higher than the 40 % risk decrease previously linked to the standard‑dose vaccine. The findings suggest that a stronger flu vaccine could offer additional protective benefits for seniors against Alzheimer’s disease.
summary: Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that receiving a high-dose influenza vaccine was associated with a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This reduction is greater than the approximately 40% risk reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds multi‑form cannabis users far more likely to have use disorder
content:
Scientists have identified a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction in a recent study of more than 17,700 adults in the United States. The research examined patterns of cannabis use across different consumption methods.

The study found that individuals who use cannabis in multiple forms—such as smoking, vaping, and edibles—exhibit dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms compared with those who primarily consume a single method. Nearly 67 % of multi‑form users met criteria for cannabis use disorder, whereas only 15 % of those who mainly consumed edibles did.
summary: Study finds multi‑form cannabis users far more likely to have use disorder.
author: Science Daily

title: Mysterious gas emissions and new fissures hint Mars may still be volcanically active
content: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures on Mars suggest the planet may not be geologically dead. Scientists say hot magma could still be active deep underground, creating hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy that might support microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
summary: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures on Mars suggest the planet may not be geologically dead. The findings indicate possible deep‑lying hot magma and hidden warmth that could provide chemical energy for microbial life beneath the surface.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find 1,000 cannabis seeds in 2,800‑year‑old Siberian Scythian tomb
content: Scientists studying a 2,800‑year‑old Siberian tomb uncovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical traces that indicate the ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating properties. The burial, which also contained evidence of elaborate rituals and animal sacrifices, provides the oldest directly dated archaeological proof of psychoactive cannabis use.
summary: Scientists investigating a 2,800‑year‑old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The find offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use and was surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds asteroid shape can change nuclear blast deflection effectiveness up to fivefold
content: Scientists report that a nuclear explosion could prevent a deadly asteroid from striking Earth, but new research warns that targeting the wrong side may backfire. The study shows an asteroid’s irregular shape can drastically alter its reaction to an X‑ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying by nearly fivefold depending on the impact angle.
summary: A nuclear explosion could be used to deflect a deadly asteroid threatening Earth. New research shows an asteroid’s irregular shape can cause deflection effectiveness to vary by almost five times depending on the angle of the X‑ray blast, meaning hitting the wrong side could lead to failure.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists discover quantum limit on electron tracking, could enable ultra-fast electronics
content: Scientists have identified a quantum limit that stops electrons from being measured with unlimited precision in both space and time. According to the researchers, this discovery could enable new control over chemical reactions and lead to electronics operating hundreds of thousands of times faster than current technology.
summary: Scientists have discovered a quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could enable manipulation of chemical reactions and the development of electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than current technology.
author: Science Daily

title: Ordnance Survey celebrates 225 years since first map, 1801 Kent map took decade
content: The 225th anniversary of the organisation’s first publication is an opportunity to celebrate its unique contribution to our sense of place In his one-paragraph short story, On Exactitude in Science, Jorge Luis Borges imagines an empire in which the level of cartographical ambition is so high that a map is made on a one-to-one scale with the imperial territory. The quest for perfect accuracy doesn’t end well. But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication. The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation, her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. During the course of the 19th century, the entirety of the British isles was meticulously mapped through fog, rain, wind and sun, in what was described as “a wild and arduous exercise”. The surveyors, armed with theodolites, measuring chains and notebooks, saw themselves as footsoldiers serving in the ranks of Reason as they brought intellectual order to the landscape.
summary: The Guardian editorial notes that Ordnance Survey is marking the 225th anniversary of its first publication. It recalls that the 1801 OS map of Kent required ten years to produce, driven by military concerns over a possible Napoleonic invasion.
author: Guardian Science

title: Baxdrostat shows blood pressure benefits lasting up to two years after use
content:
A new medication, baxdrostat, has shown unusually lasting effects on high‑blood‑pressure patients.  In a six‑ to 12‑month daily‑pill regimen, patients’ blood pressure improved, and the benefits persisted for up to two years after they stopped taking the drug.  

Doctors report that some patients no longer required any hypertension drugs and may have been cured of the condition, a result that has “stunned” clinicians.  The drug is said to reverse a common cause of high blood pressure, offering a potential long‑term solution for millions of people with the condition.
summary: Patients who took the daily pill baxdrostat for six to 12 months saw their blood pressure improve and the drug reversed a common cause of hypertension. The improvements persisted for up to two years after stopping the medication, with some patients no longer needing any hypertension drugs.
author: Guardian Science

title: Bininj rock shelter in Kakadu shows Namarrkon wielding lightning
content:
In a rock shelter in Kakadu National Park, the Bininj people have carved an image of Namarrkon, one of their most important creation ancestors. The carving shows Namarrkon’s flesh bleached away to reveal bone, stone axes fixed to his head, elbows, and knees, and a great band of lightning that extends from his ankles, over his head, and beyond.

Namarrkon’s journey from the coast to the Arnhem Land escarpment is believed to have shaped the surrounding landscape. In the great storms that sweep across the region during the wet season, the Bininj attribute the splitting of clouds, the thunder, the lightning, and the release of life‑giving rain to Namarrkon’s stone axes.

The depiction underscores the Bininj belief that Namarrkon’s power over thunder and lightning is integral to the creation and sustenance of their environment.
summary: Humans have always been awed by the power and beauty of lightning. How does the experience and understanding of it change in a warming world?
author: Guardian Science

title: NASA Calls for New Generation of Astronauts to Live and Work on the Moon
content:
NASA has announced a call for a new generation of astronauts who could live and work on the moon. Applications are open until 3 December as part of the latest expansion of the Artemis program.  

The agency says successful candidates will help “shape humanity’s future in space” by building a lunar base and preparing for the first crewed missions to Mars.
summary: NASA has opened applications for a new generation of astronauts to live and work on the moon, with the deadline on 3 December. Successful candidates will help shape humanity's future in space as the agency builds a lunar base and prepares for the first crewed missions to Mars.
author: Guardian Science

title: APOD features major fireball meteor captured over Italy on Nov 8 2026
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day for November 8, 2026 features a photograph taken on 14 November 2017 from a mountain pass in the Dolomite Alps of Italy. The image shows snowy, rugged peaks above the village of La Villa, Alta Badia, with the twilight sky rendered in soft pinkish hues. The constellation Ursa Major, including the Big Dipper asterism, is visible on the northern horizon.

During the camera’s exposure a bright fireball meteor crossed the sky from east to west, flashing above the village lights. The meteor was captured serendipitously in the same frame as the landscape. The event was reported widely across European skies, making it one of the most reported fireball occurrences recorded by the American Meteor Society and the International Meteor Organization.

Analysis of the meteor’s measured track over Germany indicates a trajectory consistent with an origin near the active radiant of the Northern Taurid meteor shower, which is associated with dust from Encke’s comet. The APOD entry credits the photograph to Ollie Taylor and lists Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, and Keighley Rockcliffe as authors and editors. The service is provided by ASD at NASA/GSFC, NASA Science Activation, and Michigan Tech.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

title: NASA launches $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge for U.S. schools
content:
NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge on Sunday during a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. The competition, launched as part of a Golden Age of Science, invites student teams from U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools to submit designs for the Moon Base. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that the agency is seeking students who can think creatively, work as a team, and address real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon, emphasizing that curiosity and the willingness to tackle hard problems are essential qualities for building what comes next.

The Moon Base is being developed in the lunar South Pole region, where astronauts will live, work, and explore. A permanent human presence on the Moon is described as paving the way for future crewed missions to Mars and requiring talent from various industries and backgrounds. Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, noted that the agency wants to leverage ingenuity and innovation to consider every need for explorers living and working on the lunar surface. He expressed anticipation for the fresh perspectives and bold ideas that students will bring to the project, stating that the Moon Base is ultimately for the next generation who will experience a world where humans remain on the Moon.

The multiphase challenge supports NASA’s commitment to cultivating the technical skills of tomorrow’s aerospace workforce. Student teams are tasked with designing innovative solutions across six specific categories: power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks, and astronaut safety. The challenge provides participants with an opportunity to develop skills necessary for careers in the space industry while helping to advance new concepts for Moon Base technologies.

Participants must register for the challenge through the NASA STEM Gateway, with registration open until January 25, 2027. The challenge addresses authentic environmental and mission design parameters for life and operations on the lunar surface. Deliverables reflect industry skills such as trade studies, concept proposals, and stakeholder briefings, allowing participants across technical, vocational, and various academic tracks to build career-relevant skills without requiring prior specialized engineering or technical experience.

Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters, described students as the next generation of explorers and innovators whose unique perspectives are key to envisioning a future away from Earth. The Office of STEM Engagement designed the challenge in collaboration with the Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. Complete competition details, eligibility requirements, and official rules are available at moonbasechallenge.org.
summary: Artist’s concept depicting astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems, and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at the Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. Credit: NASA On Sunday, NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida.
