title: UV-Tracking Necklace Gem Alerts Wearer to High Sun Exposure During LA Heat
content:
During a relative’s outdoor party in August, temperatures in Los Angeles reached the 90s. The writer sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan, assuming protection from the heat. After about thirty minutes, the writer experienced exhaustion, dizziness, nausea, and general illness—symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

At the same time, a notification from an app linked to a $249 (later $149) UV‑tracking necklace called Gem, manufactured by The90, alerted the wearer that UV exposure had risen significantly. The alert coincided with the onset of the writer’s heat‑related symptoms.
summary: The author wore a Gem UV‑tracking necklace from The90, priced at $249 ($149 at time of publication), while attending a relative’s outdoor party in Los Angeles in August. The necklace’s app notified the author that UV exposure had risen sharply as they experienced heat‑exhaustion symptoms.

content:
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta includes a flag for a “Conversational Apps” category, suggesting Apple may enable chatbot support on its HomeView smart‑home hub. title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders sue AI music firm Suno over voice cloning
content:
Sun​o, an AI music company, is being sued in two separate actions. One suit is brought by a group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music, and the other by the publisher of several of Eminem’s major records. Both parties allege that Sun​o illegally generates music and lyrics that imitate the respective artists.

In the Presley case, the plaintiffs’ lawyers contend that Sun​o has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which prohibits an AI firm from cloning a singer’s voice. They further argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard‑work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for …”. The lawsuits claim the company’s technology infringes on the artists’ protected rights.
summary: Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists.

title: British soldier court-martialed after refusing to remove SIM card, blackmailed
content:
An Estonian newspaper reported that British soldier Daniel Barton‑Kennedy ignored a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a location in Estonia about 90 miles west of the Russian border. After refusing the operational‑security measure, his phone was hacked, nude photographs were stolen and used to blackmail him.

Barton‑Kennedy was subsequently court‑martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pleaded guilty, was reduced in rank and sentenced to ten months’ detention.
summary: British soldier court-martialed after refusing to remove SIM card, blackmailed.

title: Scientists study Great Zimbabwe iron furnaces to trace Bantu expansion impact
content:
Scientists continue to investigate how the Bantu expansion reshaped Africa, seeking evidence of the cultural and technological changes it brought. One focus of current research is the iron‑working expertise demonstrated by the ancient inhabitants of Great Zimbabwe, the capital of a prosperous southern‑African kingdom that flourished from roughly 1000 to 1700 AD.

Archaeologists have identified clusters of iron‑smelting furnaces near the stone ruins of Great Zimbabwe, now visible as mounds of rubble. At the nearby village of Mashava, about 25 miles northwest, fragments of furnace interiors retain the fingerprints of the workers who once smoothed the clay. Some furnaces measured nearly an adult’s arm span across and featured thick walls capable of containing temperatures above 2,100 °F, sufficient to melt iron ore. Unlike many contemporary furnaces that required manual bellows, these structures drew air in and expelled it through a chimney, eliminating the need for human labor and facilitating the production of tools such as hoes, axes and arrowheads.
summary: Scientists are still tracing how the Bantu expansion changed Africa. The iron‑smelting furnaces at Great Zimbabwe, a capital from 1000‑1700 AD, were large self‑ventilating structures that produced iron for hoes, axes and arrowheads without using bellows.
author: Ars Technica

title: Physicists use electrical noise to probe cuprate pseudogap
content: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. Read full article Comments
summary: Physicists Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University measured the faint electrical crackle from current flowing into a cuprate to study its pseudogap. Their recent Science study reports that the pseudogap involves missing electrons above the superconducting temperature, offering new clues to high‑temperature superconductivity.

title: Companies launch kid-focused phones as parents seek safer alternatives
content: Parents are seeking alternatives to unrestricted smartphones for their children. In response, a growing number of companies are developing phones designed specifically for kids, offering options that range from feature‑limited mobile devices to minimalist home phones.

title: Leaked docs reveal Cisco expanded Israeli military contracts amid Gaza war
content:
Leaked documents reveal that Cisco intensified its dealings with Israel’s military intelligence during the Gaza war, despite internal protests by workers over the company’s involvement. The tech conglomerate “leaped to shore up” its relationship with the Israeli agencies even as the firm faced criticism from its own staff.

A year into the conflict, Israel’s military intelligence networks experienced prolonged outages, multi‑hour system crashes and failed debugging mechanisms. These persistent technical problems eroded the confidence of the intelligence agencies in Cisco, one of their primary network providers.
summary: Leaked documents show Cisco increased its deals with Israel’s military intelligence during the Gaza war. The company sought to shore up the relationship despite worker protests and repeated network outages that had eroded Israeli confidence in its services.

title: Trump administration plans four underwater datacenters off Maine and Alaska
content:
Tech companies are increasingly interested in underwater data‑center concepts, citing reduced community opposition and lower utility costs as key advantages. Elon Musk has long promoted space‑based data‑centers, but recent reports indicate a shift toward aquatic sites.

Two underwater data‑center facilities already operate off the coast of China. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is reportedly exploring plans for four proposed underwater, sealed‑pod data‑centers to be built off the shores of Maine and Alaska. The proposal reflects a growing trend to harness the natural cooling and isolation benefits of submerged environments for large‑scale computing.
summary: The Trump administration is considering building four sealed‑pod underwater datacenters off the coasts of Maine and Alaska. Two underwater datacenters already operate off China’s coast, and a Great Lakes nonprofit is preparing its own underwater facility.

title: Lanarkshire AI datacentre will rely entirely on National Grid, not renewable power
content: DataVita has revised plan for Chapelhall development to be wholly powered by 1GW of renewable energy A datacentre company that said it would power a massive AI development near Glasgow with renewable energy has admitted that the scheme will be entirely served by the National Grid. DataVita, a key plank of the UK’s AI strategy, had promised that the Lanarkshire project would draw 1GW – the equivalent output of a small nuclear reactor, or Britain’s largest windfarm – from green sources. But when the Guardian raised questions about the pledge, it said the arrangement was “subject to final commercial agreements, planning, grid and consenting processes”.
summary: DataVita said the Lanarkshire AI datacentre will be wholly served by the National Grid. The company had earlier pledged the Chapelhall project would draw 1 GW of renewable energy, but said the arrangement is subject to final commercial, planning, grid and consenting processes.

title: FAA launches first U.S. digital air traffic control towers in Florida and Alaska
content:
The Federal Aviation Administration announced that the United States’ first digital air‑traffic‑control towers are now operational. The new systems, which provide a 360‑degree view of airport operations, have been installed at Bartow Executive Airport (KBOW) in Florida and Kenai Municipal Airport (PAEN) in Alaska.  

The FAA noted that five additional regional airports are slated to receive the same technology, as the current administration moves forward with upgrades to the nation’s aging aviation infrastructure, despite some concerns that have been raised about the technology.
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration announced that digital air traffic control towers are now operational at Bartow executive airport (KBOW) in Florida and Kenai municipal airport (PAEN) in Alaska. Five additional regional airports are slated to receive the technology next.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Thailand pauses 49 datacentre projects as power, water constraints curb growth
content:
The rapid expansion of datacentre capacity in south‑east Asia has stalled. In early 2026 Thailand’s datacentre sector appeared to be booming, with the Board of Investment approving projects from TikTok, a UAE‑based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge Datacentres, amounting to a planned $27 billion in investment.

By September 2026 the momentum slowed as Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and deferred approval decisions on 117 more, citing power and water constraints and concerns over insufficient regulatory and monitoring details. The slowdown is not isolated. In Indonesia, the governor of West Java halted construction on a datacentre because permits were lacking and the environmental assessment process was incomplete. These actions reflect growing scrutiny of datacentre development in the region.
summary: Thailand halted construction on 49 datacentre projects and paused approval of 117 projects in September 2026 due to power, water constraints and regulatory concerns. In West Java, Indonesia, the provincial governor stopped a datacentre build because of missing permits and an incomplete environmental assessment.
author: Guardian Technology

title: 78‑year‑old Philadelphia professor Carolyn Marvin blocks food‑delivery robots
content: Semi-retired professor Carolyn Marvin became a local celebrity facing down Philadelphia’s growing robot delivery army: ‘It’s my first amendment right to protest’ “One of you needs to be on the lookout for cops, while I block the robot, OK?” It is a crisp fall morning in Philadelphia. Tucked away in a dingy alley, opposite a garage called Patriot Parking, 78-year-old Carolyn Marvin is laying out some ground rules for a robot-disrupting expedition. Once a suitable target is identified, we will follow it to a busy sidewalk and Marvin will stand in front of the robot, blocking its way. The photographer and I will take turns ensuring we’re not all carted off by the police.
summary: Semi‑retired professor Carolyn Marvin, a 78‑year‑old local celebrity in Philadelphia, confronts the city’s robot food‑delivery fleet by standing in front of the machines. She says it is her First Amendment right to protest and works with a photographer to avoid police intervention.
author: Guardian Technology

title: UK public bodies face surge of AI‑generated complaints, says Labour MP caseworker
content:
UK public bodies—including MPs, local authorities, lawyers and schools—are reporting a surge of complaints, requests and legal challenges that appear to be generated by artificial‑intelligence chatbots. Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, says the volume began as a “trickle in 2024” and has grown into an “onslaught.”  

Wickens notes that about half of the emails her office receives are some form of AI‑produced correspondence, making the material “much more complex and time‑consuming to read and deal with” despite her decade of experience. She describes the workload as “definitely more taxing.”
summary: MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and other public bodies are receiving a flood of AI‑generated grievances, requests and legal challenges. Senior caseworker Hollie Wickens of a Labour MP’s office says about half of the emails they receive are AI‑generated, making the correspondence more complex and time‑consuming to read and handle.

title: London wholesaler spots 150°C defrost lights on two fridges amid rising cyber‑attack fears
content:
The piece asks whether recent incidents – hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6 billion heist – signal the start of a broader hacking epidemic. It notes that, as AI highlights weaknesses in IT systems and geopolitics unfolds on the cyber front, some experts warn that such events could become routine.

In a concrete example, Alex Pearce was conducting his morning rounds at a fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London when he saw the defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 illuminated and the panel reading 150 °C; unit 4 showed the same readings.
summary: Alex Pearce observed the defrost lights on refrigeration units 2 and 4 at his London fruit and vegetable wholesale business were on, with panel readings of 150 °C. Experts say recent cyber incidents such as fake nuclear alerts and a $6 bn heist suggest a growing hacking threat.

content: Egypt announced the discovery of a new Mediterranean gas field with an estimated reserve of 200 billion cubic feet. The Ministry of Petroleum said the positive outcome reflects higher investment and exploration activity, an improved investment climate, and progress in settling overdue payments to foreign energy‑sector companies.
summary: Egypt announced the discovery of a new Mediterranean gas field estimated at 200 billion cubic feet. title: Egypt reopens Tripoli embassy after 12 years, objects to Turkey-Libya maritime deal
content: Egypt has reopened its embassy in Tripoli after a 12‑year closure as it seeks closer ties with Libya’s western government, shifting from its previous support for the eastern rival. In Tripoli, officials discussed energy projects and voiced Egypt’s objections to Libya’s maritime agreement with Turkey.

content: At least four people were killed and 88 injured when two trains collided about 52 kilometres south of Cairo, with one train striking the rear of the other and causing a derailment. Egyptian President Abdelfatah al‑Sisi has ordered an investigation to determine the causes and responsibility.
summary: At least four people were killed and 88 were injured when one train hit the rear of another about 52 kilometres south of Cairo, causing a derailment. President Abdelfatah al‑Sisi ordered an investigation to determine the causes and responsibility.

title: Hackers claim Rosstat data shows 393,000‑450,000 Russian deaths in Ukraine war
content: Hacker groups Cyberpartisans BY and Silent Crow say they breached Russia’s statistical agency Rosstat and compiled figures on Russian casualties since the invasion of Ukraine. Their analysis puts the death toll between 393,000 and 450,000 people.
summary: Hacker groups Cyberpartisans BY and Silent Crow say they hacked Rosstat and counted Russian losses since the invasion of Ukraine. They estimate the number of Russian deaths at between 393,000 and 450,000.

content: Azerbaijan celebrated on Sunday its sixth Victory Day, marking the end of the Karabakh war. Turkey's Erdoğan joined the commemorations to underscore the strength of bilateral ties despite recent differences, with Aliyev declaring that "this unity will last forever".

content: French sailor Tom Laperche, 29, won the Route du Rhum, crossing the finish line in Guadeloupe on his first attempt. His time set a new record for the transatlantic yacht race, beating the 2022 record by about six hours.

title: Poland launches terror probe after six killed in Krakow shooting
content: Poland on Sunday launched a terror probe into the mass shooting in Krakow the day before, in which six people were killed and many more were injured. Authorities have said that the 24-year-old suspect, who used a semi-automatic rifle in his killing spree, was “fascinated by far-right ideologies”. He is currently in critical condition in hospital. FRANCE 24 journalist Adrien Sariat reports from Poland.
summary: Poland opened a terror investigation into a mass shooting in Krakow that left six people dead and many injured. Authorities said the 24‑year‑old suspect, who used a semi‑automatic rifle and is fascinated by far‑right ideologies, is in critical condition in hospital.

title: US voters reject most AI data centre measures in midterm elections
content:
In Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, voters considered more than 40 local measures concerning AI data‑centre projects and rejected them in every case except one. The outcomes reflect a broad rejection of new data‑centre construction at the ballot box.

The defeats come as Democrats are set to control Congress in January, while newly elected governors in Texas and Georgia have announced calls for moratoriums on AI data‑centre development, marking a significant political challenge for the industry’s expansion.
summary: In Tuesday’s US midterm elections, voters rejected all but one of more than 40 local measures on AI data centres. Democrats took control of Congress in January and the new governors of Texas and Georgia have called for moratoriums, creating a tough political test for the AI building boom.

content: FRANCE 24 has compiled a visual recap of the week, featuring images of the Democratic Party’s large victories in the United States midterm elections, the ongoing student‑led protests across France, and the inaugural Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, marking the first Olympic sports event held on African soil.

content: Spanish tennis star Carlos Alcaraz defeated American Ben Shelton to claim his first Paris Masters title, avenging a September US Open loss to Shelton. The victory moved Alcaraz ahead of his rival on Sunday, while it marked Shelton’s first defeat in a Masters final.
summary: Spanish tennis star Carlos Alcaraz beat American player Ben Shelton to win the Paris Masters, his first title at the event. The win avenged Alcaraz's September US Open loss and was Shelton's first defeat in a Masters final.

title: Israel's opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot tasked with forming new government
content:
Israel’s opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been formally tasked with forming the country’s next government after President Isaac Herzog announced the mandate. Eisenkot has up to six weeks to negotiate with potential coalition partners and secure a parliamentary majority.

The report notes that an alliance with Arab Israeli parties would be the mathematically simplest path to a majority, though it is described as politically sensitive. Eisenkot’s negotiations aim to build a coalition capable of replacing Benjamin Netanyahu, according to Noga Tarnopolsky reporting from Jerusalem.
summary: Gadi Eisenkot has been officially assigned by President Isaac Herzog to build Israel's next government. He has up to six weeks to negotiate coalition partners, with an Arab Israeli party alliance seen as mathematically easiest but politically sensitive, as he aims to replace Benjamin Netanyahu.

title: Russian airstrikes cut power for hundreds of thousands in Ukraine
content: Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians lost electricity on Sunday after Russian airstrikes hit the country’s energy infrastructure. The attacks, which Moscow has intensified as winter approaches, have left residents in Kyiv and other regions coping with power cuts amid falling temperatures, according to reporter Clemence Waller.
summary: Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians were left without electricity on Sunday after Russian airstrikes hit the country's energy infrastructure. The attacks, which Moscow has intensified as winter approaches, left residents in Kyiv and other areas coping with power cuts as temperatures drop.

title: Democrats consider next moves after Republicans lose congressional majority
content: Donald Trump’s Republican Party has lost its majority in both the House and the Senate, giving Democrats a congressional win in the midterms. While the president retains significant authority, Democratic leaders have not yet reached consensus on how to deploy their newfound power.
summary: Donald Trump's Republican party has lost its majority in both chambers of the US Congress. The president still has a lot of power — and the Democrats have yet to agree on how best to use theirs.

content: Reza Pahlavi, the son of Iran’s deposed monarch, was presented with a “Freedom Prize” in Frankfurt before a crowd of about 18,000 supporters. Some opposition factions have criticized him for not distancing himself from his father’s rule.
summary: Reza Pahlavi, son of Iran’s former monarch, was awarded a Freedom Prize in Frankfurt before a crowd of about 18,000 supporters. Some opposition factions have criticized him for not distancing himself from his father’s rule.

content: Ebola has been known for decades, yet there is still no vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain driving the current outbreak. New research, however, is reported to raise hopes of achieving protection against the various types of Ebola.

content: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, recorded its worst‑ever result in South Africa’s municipal election. Voters attributed the outcome to the ANC’s handling of water and electricity shortages.

content: High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome... That people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks. content: National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc. title: Thailand to deport two Uyghurs to China, activists say they face slavery
content:
Activists warn that Bangkok may yield to Beijing’s pressure, even as reports of torture and other human‑rights abuses against the predominantly Muslim Uyghur minority circulate.

The potential deportation of two more Uyghurs would place their lives in grave danger, activists say. One of the men said he would be “like a slave” if sent back. Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN. The US and Canada had offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared intent on avoiding upsetting Beijing. The UN reports the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
summary: Thailand to deport two Uyghurs to China, activists say they face slavery.

title: Pope Leo XIV visits Argentine disability home as President Milei cuts funding
content: President has opposing views on many issues, and once called Leo’s predecessor the ‘representative of the Evil One’ Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina. But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.
summary: Pope Leo XIV will begin his first full day in Argentina on Monday 9 November with a visit to the Cottolengo Don Orione home for disabled people in Claypole, about 26 km from Buenos Aires. content:
The event “See My World” will showcase pan‑African thought through film, poetry and dance, drawing on momentum generated by local activists and creatives. Organisers say African philosophies—particularly reflections on how past lessons can influence the present and near future—have inspired a new approach to staging a film festival in Manchester.

“See My World” is a day‑long program dedicated to independent creators from the African diaspora in the north of England and is scheduled for 21 November at the Contact theatre.

content:
A train collision in Egypt’s al‑Ayyat district, about 30 miles south of Cairo, killed at least seven people and injured more than 100, officials said. The accident occurred on Sunday when a train bound for the south‑western Fayoum province struck the rear of a train traveling toward the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

content:

title: UKFPU prioritizes antisocial behavior by teenage ultras in non-league football
content: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it. The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?
summary: The UK Football Policing Unit has declared antisocial behavior by teenage ultras its most important priority due to increasing disorder in non-league football. Communities fear that current trouble-making by groups like the "schooligans" will eventually become more dangerous.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Study finds childcare's effect on child napping reverses as kids age
content:
A well‑napped child is often described as cheerful and happy. In a society where both parents typically work, most children attend childcare during their first five years—a period that coincides with the shift from regular daytime naps to sleeping through the night.

A recent study published in Sleep Medicine examined whether attending childcare alters the number of naps a child takes in a day compared with days spent at home. The research also explored how this relationship changes as children age.
summary: A well-napped child is a cheerful and happy child. In a world where both parents have to work, most children spend their first five years attending childcare, right around the time they transition from regular daytime naps to sleeping through the night.

title: Cyber‑attack heats European supermarket freezers, causing food loss worth millions
content: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers. Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses. The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe. Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War : The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World
summary: A cyber‑attack switched supermarket freezers from “freeze” to “defrost” across Europe, raising temperatures to about 50 °C and forcing the disposal of food worth millions of euros. Russian hacktivists claimed responsibility, though Iran, North Korea or unaffiliated hackers are also possible, and a similar hack previously hit Transport for London by two British teenagers.

title: SpaceX launches classified USSF-432 mission from Vandenberg
content:
SpaceX executed a classified launch for the U.S. Space Force on November 6, sending a Falcon 9 rocket into orbit from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The liftoff occurred at 7:48 p.m. EST, coinciding with a sunset over the Pacific Ocean. Designated as the USSF-432 mission, the flight remained largely undisclosed by both SpaceX and the Space Force prior to launch. During the broadcast, SpaceX ended its webcast approximately ten minutes into the flight, shortly after the rocket’s first stage separated and began its return to Earth.

The Falcon 9’s first stage, booster 1095, successfully landed on the SpaceX droneship “Of Course I Still Love You,” which was positioned downrange in the Pacific Ocean. This event marked the eighth flight for this specific booster. Meanwhile, the rocket’s upper stage continued its ascent, carrying a mystery payload that observers speculate may be destined for low Earth orbit. External analysts suggest the payload could be a batch of classified satellites for the Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, potentially built on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite bus.

This launch represented the 119th Falcon 9 mission of 2026 and the 14th national-security flight for the rocket that year. In 2026, more than 70% of Falcon 9 missions have been dedicated to expanding the Starlink megaconstellation, which currently includes more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a related system designed to provide services to the U.S. Military and its allies, with satellites believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus.

Beyond the Falcon 9, SpaceX has conducted six other missions in 2026. These include three operational flights of the Falcon Heavy rocket and three test missions of the next-generation Starship vehicle. The company plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets once the fully reusable Starship, described as the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is fully operational.
summary: SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U. S.

title: Genetic variant may increase pneumonia risk, study finds
content:
A new study published in eBioMedicine indicates that genetic differences within the innate immune system can influence the risk of developing pneumonia. Researchers from Lund University and Skåne University Hospital conducted this investigation, adding a genetic dimension to the understanding of the disease.

Pneumonia is a common and sometimes serious infection that affects 20,000–30,000 people annually in Sweden. While advanced age, smoking, and underlying medical conditions are well-known risk factors, the study highlights that genetic variants may also play a significant role in susceptibility to the infection.
summary: Researchers at Lund University and Skåne University Hospital found that genetic differences in the innate immune system can influence the risk of developing pneumonia. The study, published in eBioMedicine, adds to known risk factors such as advanced age, smoking, and underlying medical conditions.

content: A paper in Nature reports that an AI system can detect hypertension by interpreting sensor readings from a consumer smartwatch. Tests of the system show it achieves sensitivities similar to traditional office-based blood pressure screening methods.

title: Gene therapy shows sustained efficacy four years after treatment for Crigler-Najjar syndrome
content:
The New England Journal of Medicine has published a study evaluating the long‑term efficacy of AAV8‑mediated gene therapy (GNT0003) in patients with Crigler‑Najjar syndrome. The report shows that the therapy’s benefits are maintained four years after treatment.  

Crigler‑Najjar syndrome is an extremely rare congenital liver disorder that affects roughly 500 people in Europe. It results from a deficiency of the enzyme UGT1A1, which is required for bilirubin metabolism. When bilirubin accumulates, it can cause irreversible neurological damage and, in the most severe cases, death.
summary: The New England Journal of Medicine has published a study on the long-term efficacy of AAV8-mediated gene therapy (GNT0003) in patients with Crigler-Najjar syndrome, an extremely rare congenital liver disorder affecting approximately 500 people in Europe. It is caused by a deficiency of UGT1A1, an enzyme required for bilirubin metabolism.

title: High-precision timeline helps clarify an ancient magma surge in the North Cascades
content: A new high‑precision timeline has shed light on an ancient magma surge that occurred in the North Cascades. The study focuses on continental arcs, which form where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust. These arcs can experience episodic magma flare‑ups, with magma flow into the continental crust increasing up to 20 times the normal rate. The surges can last tens of millions of years, but the exact triggers for these extreme events remain unclear.
summary: Where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, belts of volcanoes known as continental arcs can form. Located around the world, these arcs may undergo episodic magma flare-ups—dramatic surges in the flow of magma into the continental crust at rates up to 20 times higher than normal.

title: Iran-linked tankers loiter near Gulf of Oman undersea cables amid warnings to Trump
content:
Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been observed loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz. Maritime intelligence firm Windward tracked the movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat in October, according to the Financial Times. The activity has been described as a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed U.S. and Israeli strikes.

Six active cables currently cross the contested Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Middle East with Europe, Africa and Asia. Two additional cables have segments under construction in the region. Four countries—Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar—depend entirely on subsea telecommunications links that run through the Strait to reach the outside world. Other nations also rely heavily on the region’s cable network; for example, one‑third of India’s westbound Internet traffic passes through the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
summary: Three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat were tracked by Windward near major undersea cables in the Gulf of Oman in October. The movements suggest Iran may be preparing to attack subsea infrastructure in response to potential US and Israeli strikes.

title: UK man in his 20s survives knife through eye and brain, remains conscious
content:
A man in his 20s arrived at a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife protruding from his face. The 15 mm‑wide blade had passed completely through his right eye and brain, with the tip reaching the top of his skull. Despite the injury, he was alive, conscious, able to speak and move all four limbs, though he was described as agitated.

Medical staff assessed his neurological status with the Glasgow Coma Scale, recording a score of 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a moderate brain injury. Because his confused and agitated condition raised the risk that he might attempt to remove the knife himself, doctors promptly sedated and intubated him, administered prophylactic treatments for bacterial infection including tetanus, and obtained imaging to evaluate the damage.

The case was detailed in a report published on Friday in BMJ Case Report. The report outlines the immediate clinical decisions made to stabilize the patient and prevent further harm while assessing the extent of his injuries.
summary: A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.

title: I finally got my hands on the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars with augmented reality and I can’t wait to stargaze with them
content:
The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars, announced in 2024, are the first pair of smart binoculars designed specifically for night sky observation. They feature an augmented reality (AR) overlay in the right-hand lens that identifies night sky targets, including planets, stars, and deep space objects, as well as landmarks and navigational tools. The device is pre-ordered for $1,499 or £1,299 and ships with a soft carry case, padded neck strap, USB-C cable, and rubber caps for the eyepieces and lenses.

The binoculars have a solid build, though they are not the most lightweight option due to the embedded technology. They feature 10x magnification and 50mm objective lenses, which provide strong light-gathering power essential for stargazing. The control panel includes five buttons on the top: the left side controls guided tour advancement, target lock selection, and display mode, while the right side houses the calibration and power buttons, with the power button also serving as a switch for the AR display. A central focus wheel allows for manual adjustments, though it requires two hands to operate.

Setting up the device is recommended during the daytime to allow time for familiarization with the controls and diopter adjustment. After powering on, the binoculars connect to the Unistellar app, which recognizes the device and provides onboarding videos. Users are advised to perform a 360-degree calibration before first use and to set location services to "always" to ensure accurate AR readings for target locations.

In daytime testing, the topographical identification feature successfully identified local landmarks, and the target lock feature allowed a friend to easily locate a geographical landmark via the AR indicator. However, the diopter adjustment is only accurate for one person at a time, making it inconvenient to swap users during field observation. Additionally, a friend had to adjust the focus wheel to make the AR overlay sharp enough to read, a minor inconvenience noted during testing.

The reviewer has not yet tested the night mode due to cloudy skies but anticipates using the device for stargazing and teaching others about constellations. The Unistellar Envision is expected to receive additional functionality through future software updates, with a plan to allow third-party app development in 2027. The device offers distinct modes for night observation, daytime use, and navigation, the latter displaying cardinal direction alongside azimuth and elevation angles.
summary: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek.

title: German astronomer discovers Tycho supernova in 1572, initially mistaken for a new star
content: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/RIKEN & GSFC/T. Sato et al; Optical: DSS) Why it mattered The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572, is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star. While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky. "The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004. "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova." "This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time. Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis, or the Blaze Star, the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). Is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
summary: German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova in the constellation Cassiopeia with the naked eye on Nov. 6, 1572, though Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. The event, known as Tycho's Star, was visible to the naked eye for 16 months and was not classified as a supernova until the 1940s.

title: Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook review – the heir to a legendary eatery … who sets soup on fire
content:
In the cooking series Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, actor, rapper, and comedian Awkwafina navigates the kitchen with genuine bewilderment. Known by her real name, Nora Lum, within the series, she is portrayed as having no prior experience with culinary tools or techniques. The show documents her chaotic and humorous journey as she attempts to resurrect her family’s famous restaurant.

The review highlights the authenticity of Awkwafina’s lack of culinary knowledge, noting that her ignorance of how food, pans, knives, and plates work feels refreshing compared to other celebrity cooking shows where inexperience is often performed. Specific scenes illustrate her discomfort, including her crouched stance near the oven, her tentative handling of spatulas and ladles, and her visible aversion to raw ingredients.

content:

Lelio is identified as one of the standard bearers of the Novisimo Cine Chileno, or New Chilean Cinema, a movement that includes directors Pablo Larraín, Patricio Guzmán, and Sebastián Silva.

The text notes that the last two decades have seen a significant rise in creativity from Chilean filmmakers. These directors brought global attention to the nation’s history, including the period of Augusto Pinochet’s rule, which the article characterizes as a tyranny enabled by the United States as an alternative to communism. The filmmakers also depicted the transition to a prosperous democratic normality where collective trauma and guilt persisted.

Lelio’s work is characterized as fierce, passionate, and sensual, with some films being explicitly political while others were not. The article argues that his films served as an expression of defiance against a system that deprived ordinary people of pleasure, effectively dramatizing the complex and conflicted zeitgeist of 21st-century Chile.

title: Wallabies struggle to turn moments into momentum despite talented squad
content:
The Wallabies possess a squad with the potential for exceptional performances, yet questions persist regarding their ability to consistently translate individual talent into sustained team success. The team frequently demonstrates moments of brilliance, such as Len Ikitau’s underhand pass to Max Jorgensen for a late try at Twickenham and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii’s run past multiple British and Irish Lions defenders. Additionally, Australia has shown resilience in high-pressure situations, including securing a victory against the Springboks while down to 11 men and defending a four-point lead with five minutes remaining.

Despite these flashes of ability, the Wallabies have struggled to maintain this level of performance over extended periods. Historical context suggests that while previous Australian teams have exhibited similar sparks, few have managed to convert them into consistent wins across consecutive matches. Recent results reflect this inconsistency, as the team lost all four Tests on their European tour last autumn and suffered two additional defeats in the summer.

Following a successful unbeaten run of six matches against Italy, Japan, Argentina, and South Africa, the Wallabies faced significant setbacks in the Bledisloe Cup. They were defeated by the All Blacks in consecutive matches, losing by 31 points in one week and 22 points the following week. These results highlight the ongoing challenge for the team to turn isolated moments of excellence into lasting momentum and revive the spirits of the squad.

content:

This condition can occur when the maternal immune response, which typically prevents fetal rejection, becomes dysregulated. The study specifically examined the immune cell landscape at the junction connecting the mother and fetus in pregnancies affected by this complication.

To map these immune cells, the team utilized spatial and single-cell gene and protein expression profiling. This approach allowed them to analyze the placenta down to individual cells, providing detailed insights into the aggressive inflammation associated with preterm cases.

title: MIT's CheMeleon model predicts molecular behavior from scant data
content:
A new method developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) demonstrates that artificial intelligence can outperform existing approaches for predicting molecular behavior when data on specific properties is limited. This development addresses the trial-and-error nature of discovering new molecules for pharmaceuticals, electronics, and energy sectors, where perfect prediction of chemical compound behavior remains elusive. The findings were published in the Sept. 14 issue of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling by MIT graduate student Akshat Shirish Zalte, recent graduate Jackson Burns PhD ’26, Research Scientist Charlles Abreu, Professor William Green, and three researchers from BASF.

The open-source model, named CheMeleon, was built using ChemProp, a machine-learning package developed and maintained by the Green group at MIT. CheMeleon is a pre-trained foundation model that utilizes molecular descriptors of one million molecules from PubChem, a freely available chemical database maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health. By pre-training on this extensive dataset, the model learns correlations between molecular structure and a catalog of approximately 1,600 descriptors developed by chemists. This process allows the system to identify underlying patterns and relationships, enabling it to apply this general chemical understanding to new, unknown molecules even when fine-tuned with only a few data points for a specific task.

Professor William Green, the Hoyt Hottel Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT, noted the model’s impact following a contest organized by OpenADMET earlier this year to predict properties of unsynthesized molecules. When the winners were announced, nine of the top 20 entries had utilized CheMeleon in their process. This success led to inquiries from pharmaceutical companies before the paper had even undergone peer review. Green stated that at least one pharmaceutical company adopted CheMeleon as its new company policy for initial molecular modeling decisions, instructing its staff to start with the tool when modeling any property.

Akshat Shirish Zalte explained that unlike many deep-learning models that require extensive data from published literature, CheMeleon does not rely on literature sources. Instead, it calculates molecular descriptors such as molecular weight and the number of oxygens. The team compared CheMeleon against other foundation models and classical expert-driven models across 58 test cases. Zalte reported that CheMeleon performed best in these comparisons. Green added that the model drastically reduces the number of molecules requiring experimental testing, offering a significant advantage given that synthesizing and testing large numbers of molecules is both slow and expensive.

The research team included Jochen Sieg, Christian Feldmann, and Miriam Mathea, researchers at BASF SE in Germany. The work was supported by the Machine Learning for Pharmaceutical Discovery and Synthesis consortium, as well as fellowship support from the U.S. Department of Energy and MathWorks. An earlier version of the paper has been available online since last year, and the model is accessible for download and fine-tuning through ChemProp.
summary: Researchers at MIT developed CheMeleon, a pre-trained foundation model that uses molecular descriptors from a million compounds to predict chemical properties with high accuracy. The open-source model outperformed other methods in 58 test cases and has been adopted by pharmaceutical companies to reduce the number of molecules requiring expensive experimental testing.

title: LDraw Mecha: Agents Infer LEGO Mechanisms from Source and Animate Them
content:
A developer has released LDraw Mecha, a new agentic tool designed to animate LEGO models by inferring their mechanical structures from source code. The project builds on the creator’s previous release, LDraw Nova, which generates LDraw source code for assembling LEGO CAD models. Following community interest in animated AI-generated LEGO models, the developer explored using agentic large language models to reverse-engineer mechanisms within existing LDraw files.

LDraw Mecha operates by reading specially annotated LDraw source files to infer the model’s structure and identify specific submodels that function as mechanisms. The system then plans animations for these components and executes them using Blender. The final output is a rigged and animated version of the original model, exported as a Blender (.blend) file.

The project is currently at version 0.5.0, with a public repository, gallery, and process documentation available on GitHub. The creator has shared the work on Hacker News, seeking community feedback on this unusual application of agentic AI in 3D animation.

title: AI data center expansion faces bipartisan backlash, polls, and new regulatory restrictions
content:
Massive new data centers serve as the physical foundation for the artificial intelligence ambitions of major technology companies, yet their rapid expansion has sparked global conflicts regarding power grids, utility bills, and environmental impacts. Data centers emerged as a significant bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, with voters largely opposing expansion at the polls. In the aftermath of the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further restrictions and slowdowns, while tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon promise to collaborate more closely with local communities and cover their own energy costs.

The political landscape surrounding these facilities has shifted dramatically, with data centers influencing the outcome of several key races. Maine Republican Susan Collins conceded her Senate seat in a tech-fueled race, while a Democrat was projected to win an Ohio seat that Republicans warned could pose problems for data center development. Additionally, Texas, a state dense with data centers, turned blue in the election. Following these results, a lame-duck Congress is considering measures to speed up energy projects, while New York became the first state to enact a data center moratorium.

Environmental and community concerns have intensified, with reports indicating that data centers could send US climate pollution skyrocketing and erase decades of air quality gains. Specific regions are facing distinct challenges; for instance, AI infrastructure is straining Arizona’s water supply, and Amazon’s data centers used 2.5 billion gallons of water last year. In Utah, a 40,000-acre data center project was approved despite community outcry, and Kevin O’Leary agreed to downsize a massive project in the state. Meanwhile, in Indiana, the mayor of Shelbyville stated that only people living in “shitty houses” oppose data centers, while Amazon employees have reported facing termination for backing data center limits.

Tech companies are responding to these pressures through various strategic moves. OpenAI has begun renaming its facilities “compute campuses” and is stepping back from non-disclosure agreements for its projects. Nvidia has guaranteed up to $105 billion to support an OpenAI data center, while Anthropic is paying $15 billion a year for access to Elon Musk’s data centers. Other major players, including Google, Meta, and Microsoft, are pursuing diverse energy solutions, such as nuclear power, geothermal energy, and vehicle-to-grid technology, to manage the immense power demands of their infrastructure.

The debate has also extended to unconventional locations and infrastructure. Elon Musk has proposed merging SpaceX and xAI to build data centers in space, a concept Google and Amazon have also explored. On the ground, the construction boom has led to a surge in gas projects to power data centers, with the Department of Justice arguing that XAI’s gas-powered facility is necessary for national security. As the industry expands, utility companies are promising to spare consumers from the full cost of AI’s energy bill, while regulators in California and other states tighten rules on energy and water usage.
summary: Voters largely opposed data center expansion in the 2026 midterms, leading Democratic leaders to call for further restrictions and slowdowns. Tech companies are responding by promising to cover energy costs and work more closely with local communities.

content: Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide ( karōjisatsu in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise: Karōshi is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface. Teo Yoo ( Past Lives ) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries Shōgun, as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu. Read full article Comments
summary: Chad Stahelski, creator of the John Wick franchise, is returning with the dystopian action film Karōshi, set in a near‑future Manhattan corporate environment. The film, written and directed by Takashi Doscher, stars Teo Yoo, Takehiro Hira, Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.

content:

The upgrade involves installing the new Enterprise Information Display System (E‑IDS) in 435 facilities, replacing several older information display systems that date back to the 1980s. E‑IDS will be deployed to operational control positions at more than 400 facilities across all air‑traffic control domains. The FAA said the system will provide operationally essential information for controlling aircraft.

title: Earth's Mantle Movements May Explain Great Unconformity Gap
content: In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.” In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior. Ice and sea The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says. title: Chainalysis reports hackers stole credentials and tokens for all customers
content:
Chainalysis, a blockchain analysis firm, announced that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The firm listed a number of high‑profile customers, such as the FBI, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the U.S. Air Force, Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It is unclear whether the theft exposes these customers to additional threats.

The company said the incident occurred in October and was similar to other hacks that month. An external actor used AI‑agent‑assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. In an email to affected customers, Chainalysis noted that “non‑sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” The firm has not explained why it classified this information as non‑sensitive.
summary: Chainalysis said hackers obtained names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all its users after a breach. The incident, which used AI‑agent‑assisted techniques, impacted customers such as the FBI, ICE, US Air Force, Microsoft, Coinbase and Barclays.

title: NASA to host first air show, Max Power, on Florida's Space Coast this weekend
content:
NASA is set to host its first-ever air show and aerospace expo, titled Max Power, on Florida’s Space Coast. The two-day event will take place on Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, at and around NASA’s Kennedy Space Center. While the name Max Power is a reference to a "Simpsons" episode where Homer adopts the alias from a hair dryer, the event itself focuses on significant aerospace developments. Tickets are required for attendance, and the schedule includes a variety of presentations, discussions, and live demonstrations.

The Saturday program features an overview of NASA’s "quiet" supersonic jet, the X-59, scheduled for 11:15 a.m. EST. Following this, Nicky Fox and Lori Glaze, heads of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate respectively, will discuss the agency’s science and exploration goals. The afternoon will include a Q&A with the four astronauts of the Artemis III mission, a session on astronaut preparation for lunar living led by Suzanne Bell of the Behavioral Health and Performance Laboratory, and a discussion on the planned lunar outpost with Moon Base program head Carlos García-Galán. The day concludes with a summary of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope mission by senior project scientist Julie McEnery.

Sunday’s schedule includes a presentation on how NASA uses aircraft for research and an update on the U.S. Space Academy by NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson. Concurrently, astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway from SpaceX’s Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station will participate in a Q&A session. Other highlights include a discussion of the SR-1 Freedom, a planned nuclear-powered spacecraft intended to launch mini-helicopters to Mars in 2028, and a session on X-Planes. The day also features a conversation with an unnamed NASA astronaut and a segment titled "In the Cockpit: Meet the NASA Pilots!"

In addition to the scheduled talks, NASA will hold a livestreamed press conference on Saturday at 5 p.m. EST regarding its moon base plans. This conference will feature Fox, García-Galán, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and Dayna Ise, the acting director of the Utility and Infrastructure Office for the Moon Base Program. The event will also include dramatic flyovers on both days, some performed by Isaacman, who is described as an accomplished pilot and private astronaut. Isaacman previously funded and commanded the SpaceX Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn missions, which flew to Earth orbit in September 2021 and September 2024, respectively.

According to the schedule, Isaacman will perform flyovers on both Saturday and Sunday at 11:58 a.m. in an F-5 jet and at 1:31 p.m. in a MiG-29. The event grounds will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, and technologies defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, while agency partners will exhibit moon rovers, spacecraft, and other equipment.
summary: NASA will host a first-of-its-kind air show and aerospace expo on Florida's Space Coast this weekend. The show, called Max Power, will take place Saturday and Sunday (Nov.

title: Midnight musical by Todrick Hall criticized for ignoring slavery-era realities
content:
Todrick Hall’s off-Broadway musical, Midnight, centers on a doomed interracial romance set during the era of US slavery in the 1860s. The production features a diverse cast and strong vocals, leading some audience members to compare it to Hamilton. However, unlike Lin-Manuel Miranda’s work, which was based on Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography of Alexander Hamilton, Hall did not utilize source material for Midnight. Instead, the creator and star of the show developed an original narrative that the review describes as neglecting the social realities of its characters.

The plot follows Rail, an enslaved man played by Hall, who falls in love with Richard, a member of the wealthy planter class. Their relationship develops after Richard rents Rail from his owner, Charlotte. Complicating the romance, Rail is in a relationship with Lily Rose, an enslaved woman, while Richard is engaged to Scarlet, a southern belle seeking to secure her family’s financial future through marriage. The story is characterized as a formulaic tale of star-crossed lovers that updates the trope to explore a queer relationship during the time of enslavement.

Hall, a singer, choreographer, and theatre actor, has previously repurposed classics such as Cinderella and Beauty and the Beast through a queer lens, often incorporating modern cultural references like Beyoncé’s music. In Midnight, however, he creates a fantasy that deviates significantly from historical accuracy. The review concludes that the musical fails to effectively imagine the intimate lives of enslaved people, noting that its premise strays so far from historical reality that it misses its intended mark entirely.
summary: Todrick Hall's off-Broadway musical Midnight depicts a doomed interracial romance between an enslaved man and a wealthy planter during the 1860s. Critics argue the show neglects the social realities of its characters by creating a fantasy that deviates from historical accuracy.

title: Wynonna Judd releases raw new album addressing mother's death and personal struggles
content: The country star has abandoned Nashville slickness for a set of raw, pared-back songs that reckon with the death of her mother and decades of personal struggles. ‘This is a labour of love,’ she says When Wynonna Judd appears on my laptop screen – hair a deep shade of crimson, makeup perfect and sporting a huge black baseball cap with Kentucky Queen spelt out across its brim – she looks both fabulous and confident. Which is a good thing, as the Nashville star has been off the radar for a decade. On the occasions her name has made the news, it’s more often been linked to family tragedy than music. “I’m in a good place,” says the woman Rolling Stone described as “the greatest female country singer since Patsy Cline”. “My life has been chaotic. I’ve had a lot of success and a lot of failure, and it’s music that keeps me going. Always.”
summary: Wynonna Judd has abandoned her polished Nashville style for a new album of raw songs that confront the death of her mother and decades of personal struggles. The country star describes the record as a labor of love that reflects her chaotic life and history of success and failure.

title: Florence Pugh Calls Dune Her Generation's Star Wars Ahead of Part Three
content: According to Florence Pugh, Denis Villeneuve’s stunningly strange and breathtaking universe is the equivalent to George Lucas’ heroic space opera. Let’s hope not A long time ago, far far away, in a galaxy called the 1970s, kids dreamed of joining the rebellion, rescuing a princess and blowing up the Death Star. Peer into the cosmic tea leaves and it would become immediately clear that no amount of evildoing could withstand a neurotic gold butler, a dustbin with ideas above its station and a walking seven-foot tall shagpile carpet with a very low tolerance for disagreement. It is worth remembering this when considering Florence Pugh’s recent declaration, ahead of next month’s Dune: Part Three, that Dune is her generation’s Star Wars. And then wondering how much trouble we might be in if she’s actually right. “I think they brought back movie-going. What an event the second [Dune] was,” Pugh cheerfully told the New York Times. “It was just so lovely to be a part of something that we know is our generational kind of Star Wars.”
summary: Florence Pugh stated that Denis Villeneuve's Dune franchise is equivalent to George Lucas' Star Wars. She made this declaration ahead of the release of Dune: Part Three, noting that the second film brought audiences back to theaters.

title: The Cat in the Hat review – Bill Hader brings plenty but this animated rework is a mess
content: The SNL alum has an appealing energy and this is an improvement on the 2003 travesty but it’s also far too long and strangely corporate Over a long enough timeline, perhaps every living alumnus of Saturday Night Live will play the Cat in the Hat. Mike Myers kicked off this unexpected tradition by embodying the furry, anarchic Dr Seuss character for a notoriously, almost defiantly ghastly 2003 live-action treatment. After doing us all the service of killing flesh-and-blood Seuss movies for good, Myers was later followed by a more charming Martin Short (via voiceover on a cute PBS/CBC animated series) and now Bill Hader, stepping into the role for a big-budget animated reboot from the oft-flailing animation division of Warner Bros. Just to be clear, this is the same studio that passed on releasing not one but two well-liked features starring their trademark Looney Tunes characters in the last few years. (Puzzlingly, a new Looney Tunes short starring Daffy Duck nonetheless debuts in front of this movie.) Warner has one of the most storied animation libraries in American cinema (and, for that matter, plenty of great animated TV shows like Batman: The Animated Series and Animaniacs) but as far as features go, they’ve never settled on a clear creative vision. They seem just as adrift in a landscape crowded with serious competitors as they were back when everyone was imitating Disney.
summary: The Cat in the Hat review – Bill Hader brings plenty but this animated rework is a mess.

title: Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg emerges as NBA’s most entertaining rookie
content:
Yaxel Lendeborg has quickly become one of the most talked‑about newcomers in the NBA. The 24‑year‑old Puerto Rican forward joined the Golden State Warriors and, in his first weeks, has been noted for antagonizing superstars, speaking his mind in the press, and drawing attention away from his teammates.

Lendeborg’s path to the league was unconventional. He spent 12 to 14 hours a day gaming and did not join his high‑school basketball team until he was an upperclassman. He also admitted that he did not really watch the NBA before entering the league. Despite this, he earned enough accolades in college to qualify for the NBA, most notably leading Michigan to its first national championship in 37 years.

The Warriors, still balancing the legacy of their 2010s dynasty with a new core, produced flashes of old greatness to win a single play‑in game before falling in the next. With veteran guard Stephen Curry still at a high level at 38, Lendeborg is seen as a key hope for the team’s future success.

In addition to his on‑court contributions, Lendeborg’s candid takes and willingness to engage with media have made him the season’s most compelling personality, a role he embraces even though he reportedly first heard the term “media training” only in college.
summary: Yaxel Lendeborg, a 24‑year‑old Puerto Rican forward for the Golden State Warriors, has spent his first weeks in the NBA antagonizing superstars and drawing media attention. He previously led Michigan to its first national championship in 37 years after not debuting on his high school basketball team until his upperclassman years.

title: Lebanon, Ukraine, and Syria Rugby Teams Compete Despite Home Wars
content:
Rugby league players from Lebanon, Syria, and Ukraine have continued to compete internationally despite ongoing conflicts in their home countries. In Sydney, Syria played a series of friendlies at the Bankstown Bulls' home ground, while Lebanon faced France in a World Cup match at CommBank Stadium. Additionally, Ukraine participated in a European Championship fixture in Belgrade. The Lebanon team secured a victory over France following a dramatic finish, a result that suggests they remain among the top eight teams globally, although their official ranking is lower due to inactivity since the last World Cup.

Prop Jalal Bazzaz, who played in all three of Lebanon’s World Cup matches, noted that the team's last gathering was in England in 2022. He stated that the players aimed to perform well each week and give back to their roots. Bazzaz described representing his country as putting Lebanon on the world stage, providing people with something to smile about and offering a sense of hope. The athletes from these war-torn nations expressed determination to give people hope, put their countries on the map, and wear their national badges with honor.
summary: Players from Lebanon, Syria, and Ukraine stated they compete to give their people hope and put their countries on the map despite ongoing wars at home. Lebanon recently defeated France in a World Cup match, while Syria and Ukraine played international fixtures in Sydney and Belgrade.

title: Saffie Osborne rides in Hong Kong after St Leger win
content:
Saffie Osborne’s year has been marked by a dramatic shift from a low point at Wolverhampton to a high-profile engagement in Hong Kong. The 24-year-old jockey began the season on 6 January by riding a 150-1 chance in a £7,000 race at Wolverhampton, where she finished last of the seven runners. Her year concludes on Sunday with a contract to ride at Sha Tin racecourse in Hong Kong, where she is scheduled to have 10 rides on an 11-race card.

The ten months between these events were described as transformational for Osborne. She achieved her first top-10 finish in the Flat jockeys’ championship, a result attributed to her consistency during the May-to-October title race. The standout achievement of her season was her September victory in the St Leger on Highwayman. This win represented Osborne’s first Group One success and marked the first time a female jockey had won a British Classic.
summary: Saffie Osborne will ride in ten races at Sha Tin in Hong Kong following a year that included her first Group One victory. The 24-year-old jockey won the St Leger on Highwayman, becoming the first female jockey to win a British Classic.

title: England players deny rift, pledge to protect Steve Borthwick
content:

The squad gathered for a meeting on Friday morning to address an article in the Times that alleged squad disharmony and characterized the environment under Borthwick as toxic.

Jamie George, who captained the team during the summer Tests, and returning skipper Maro Itoje led the discussion. The Times report claimed that a group of players were dissatisfied with Borthwick’s man management, specifically citing a clash between Ellis Genge and the head coach. The article further stated that senior players had sought clear-the-air talks with Borthwick and requested the presence of Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney.

Despite these allegations, the players rejected the narrative of internal conflict. Jamie George indicated that external criticism would serve to bring out the best in the England team. The squad’s unified stance aims to support Borthwick as they prepare for their upcoming match against Australia.
summary: England senior players held a meeting to deny reports of squad disharmony and stated they will fight to protect head coach Steve Borthwick. The team addressed a Times article alleging toxic management and clashes between players and the coach.

title: Idaho paid hunters $2,000 each to kill 12 newborn wolf pups
content:
State records shared with the Guardian and Public Domain reveal that Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars to kill a dozen newborn wolf pups this spring. The documents indicate a payout of $2,000 per kill, including the apparent elimination of at least one full litter in or near its den. These actions have incensed wildlife advocates across the state.

The killings occurred as part of an effort to shrink Idaho’s re-introduced wolf population. State wildlife officials have been ordered to implement extraordinary measures to reduce the number of wolves, a directive driven by complaints from the livestock industry and big game hunting outfitters.
summary: State records show Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars to kill a dozen newborn wolf pups this spring. Wildlife advocates are incensed by the killings, which occurred as part of an effort to shrink the state's re-introduced wolf population.

title: Juneau food supply relies on water, air, and community sharing
content:
In Juneau, Alaska’s capital, food is typically transported by water, air, or through community sharing. The city faces significant agricultural challenges, including limited arable land, a short growing season, and a small number of farmers. These conditions are complemented by deep traditions where residents and the land mutually support each other’s sustenance.

Forty miles northwest of the capital, the highway terminates at the northernmost point of Glacier Highway. There, the pavement transitions to gravel, which widens into a turnaround before the tire tracks curve back. At this remote end, the woods begin, with a narrow hiking trail leading toward the southern end of Berners Bay.
summary: Juneau faces limited arable land, a short growing season, and few farmers, forcing food to arrive by water or air. The city also maintains deep traditions of residents and the land feeding each other through community sharing.
